There was a proposal which I presented a few days ago with regard to the Public Accounts Committee, which, I understood, was to come up this afternoon. I move:
Thalt the public accounts of the fiscal year ending 31st March, 1910, and volumes one and two of the Auditor General's Report of the same period be referred to the Select Standing Committee on Public Accounts.

I gave notice the other day that I proposed to move an amendment to this motion. The same question was before the House a year ago and many hon. members have been considering the matter since and have become impressed with the necessity of a wider range of investigation before the Public Accounts Committee. The right hon. gentleman who leads the House (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) was good enough then to say that the remarks I addressed to the House had so impressed him and that the proposition looked so reasonable, that he would like' further time to consider it. Upon that understanding, the matter was allowed to stand over. I thought then that, inasmuch as on that occasion only the first and third volumes of the Auditor General were referred to the committee, when a motion was made to refer the second volume to the committee, the right hon. gentleman would seize upon that occasion as a fitting one in which to have the matter brought before the House again. I found, however, that the second volume was not laid on the table for nearly a month and a half and that, strange to say, it was never referred to the Eublie Accounts Committee. I then got busy with other matters, very interesting to me and I believe also very interesting to the country, and the one to which I am now referring escaped further discussion last year. The right hon. gentleman and others have had an opportunity of considering the question in the meantime, and I entertain the hope that the Prime Minister will now, in harmony with the suggestion which he threw out last year, see fit to let the amendment go through without^ a vote. What I am moving for is that instead of having only the accounts for the last financial year ending March 31, last, referred to the Public Accounts Committee, we shall refer to it the accounts of last year and the accounts of the preceding year, together with the Auditor General's Reports for those two years; and I do so because, in my experience and that of other hon. members, occasions arise when it is necessary to go back further than one year. And if we keep in mind the great object to be served, namely that'the people should know what their representatives are doing with the people's money, it does not seem at all unreason-

able that we should have at least two years' accounts referred to the committee. This is a reform I am asking, and it is one of a good long list required in the Public Accounts Committee. For instance I have no quarrel with the chairman -that is the chairman we have now-he is a very desirable chairman as compared with those we have had on some previous occasions, but I feel all the same that we could make an improvement as regards the question of chairmanship. Does it not seem that when these accounts are the accounts of the government and when there is a majority of the committee supporting the government, it would be more seemly, more in accord with the fitness of things and more likely to let the people know exactly what is being done by the government, if we had a chairman selected by the men who are mainly active in investigating our public accounts. That is the practice followed in England. The right hon. gentleman is very eloquent at times in pointing to British precedent particularly if it is against an argument advanced by the other side. The right hon. gentleman is disposed to follow British precedent when it suits him, but when it does not suit him he follows it at a very respectful distance. What does the right hon. gentleman think of that as a precedent? Would it not be apt to give the people a better chance of knowing what the government is doing? Would it not be calculated to give the people more confidence in the audit supposed to take place in the Public Accounts Committee? Well, I will come again next year, the Prime Minister will have time to consider it in the meantime, and if when I come next year, we have not had a general election in the meantime, I shall appeal to the right hon. gentleman, and if we have had a general election, I will appeal to the hon. leader of the opposition, as to whether it would not be better to have this reform brought about.
There are other improvements that we ought to have; one of them was suggested last year; that is, in regard to the enormous number of men we have on this committee. Does the right hon. the First Minister realize that it is absolutely impossible .ever to have efficient work done in this committee so long as we have 82 men supposed to do the work? So, when I come again next year, I hope I shall be-if we have a general election, I certainly shall be -appealing to the hon. leader of the opposition, who will then be the Prime Minister, for that reform as well.
Which one?

My hon. friend interjects which one, and that is because we have such a wealth of material on this side of the House. On the other side of the House there would be no question which one, because there is only one man who measures Mr. LENNOX.
at all up to the position. I may be told that the present method has been adopted for years and has been sanctioned by the Conservative party. I admit it, but I do not care. We are living in a progressive age; but as regards giving the people a chance to look in at what is being done, we are not living under a progressive government. I am in favour of giving the people a chance, through their representatives of auditing the public accounts fairly and ks fully as the circumstances will admit. And again what might be a tolerable system in 1896, when our total expenditures did not exceed $44,000,000, and when abuses were rare, suggestions^ of dishonesty were rare, and proof of dishonesty was rarer still, becomes an intolerable system and a great danger when we are spending, according to the estimates brought down, with supplementary estimates which may be added, no less, perhaps, than $144,000,000, and when startling and cogent evidence of dishonesty and graft assails us from every side. And what might be a fair and workable system in 1896, when supporters of the government vied with members of the opposition as auditors on behalf of the people to drag to light any isolated cases of dishonesty or wrong-doing that might have arisen, becomes intolerable when we have members of the government assembling in the Public Accounts Committee and concurring in, and sanctioning, if not conniving at, a system of premeditated and organized opposition such as we have witnessed in that committee in the last ten years. So we need not go back to 1896 to find an answer to my argument. It may be said, why not come to the House from time to time as occasion arises?
Hear, hear.

The hon. gentleman who says hear, hear, may not be in the habit of attending the Public Accounts Committee. We cannot come to the House when the occasion arises, because we are met by the rule that forbids discussion in the House upon a matter pending before a committee; when we move in the committee for enlarged powers, we are voted down; when we move to have the matter referred to the House, we are met with the statement that unless we close the investigation, and therefore render our application to the House useless, we cannot refer it to the House. So we are on the horns of a dilemma, either to refer the matter to the House and have nothing to deal with, or to take the measure of justice accorded by the committee, which is no justice at all. Again, I would not want to refer it to the House from time to time, for this reason: Do the members of the government, when they talk about hastening the session, really mean it? Do they want short sessions? If they do,

why have applications from day to day or week to week,.or even two or three in a session, which will involve half a day's discussion, when the matter could be settled at once by allowing sufficient latitude to the Public Accounts Committee. If the Prime Minister would come up and see what takes place in that Public Accounts Committee during one week, especially if the committee did not know it was being watched, he would do more good than he has done in three sessions in the House of Commons, by reforming the methods followed there. Members realize that if an investigation can be staved off till near the end of the session, it will not be held at all, and the result is- that the matter is talked out. It rarely happens that a public work has been commenced, finished and paid for in the same financial year, and it is not until an account runs into the second or third year that the figures take on form and colour, and that the sinister significance of some of the payments begins to manifest itself. So, if we are confronted with the rule that we can investigate only the transactions of a single year, we have perhaps to plunge into the middle of a transaction that has no beginning and that may have no end at that time. We are bound by this artificial rule, which never had any origin in sound principle, and is utterly unreasonable when transactions aTe so numerous and so gigantic as those that relate to Canada at the present time. I was going to say that we had a lot of free traders on the other side of the House. I do not know whether we have any or not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We have some on the other side now.

That is good. We have some gentlemen on this side of the House who do, to a very much greater extent than the hon. members on that side of the House, realize what is the true meaning of the National Policy and if that is what the First Minister means I quite agree with him. But we have the men who were for years talking about pulling down your walls and letting down your bars and all that kind of thing, principally to let the products of the United States come in and overrun the markets of the Dominion of Canada. What do you say to taking down the wall now, removing these bars and letting the people have a look in, the people whose moneys are being spent? Would it not be reasonable, is there any good reason why it should not be done? I have heard the right hon. the leader of the House (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) talk of Haman's gallows, its immense height; he and his government in the Public Accounts Committee have builded a wall against the people to shut the people out from a knowledge of their transactions, many of them nefarious, many of them dishonest, many
of them of a charatcer which could not be defended, if they came to light-he and they have builded a wail higher than Haman's gallows and thicker and far stronger than the walls of the Laurier tower which fell down a few years ago, and behind that wall there cower such men as the double named Leopold Lazarus, the North Atlantic Trading Company, ,the men of the Carbide Companies and the Sub-Target Gun Company and the Robbins Irrigation Company, the Adamson's and the Burrows, and the Walbergs and the Pearsons and the Lodges and the Mer-wins and I think the Dodges, and the Mc-Avity's and the Galloway herd, all feeding at the public trough at the expense of the people of this country. Does the right hon. gentleman want that kind of. thing to continue? The 82 men who are appointed on that committee are 82 auditors appointed to look after the peoples' money, to audit the public accounts, to get at the bottom of things, to find out what has been done and to tell the people. That is constitutionally our position. Has it been done? We on this side of the House have striven to do it, but have been blocked and prevented by hon. gentlemen supporting my right hon. friend. I will ask the Prime Minister, I will ask hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, to take a review and say how many of them can stand up and say that they have discharged their duty as auditors on behalf of the public in investigating the public accounts, ascertaining how the public money has been spent and have carried to the people, as far as they could, a knowledge of what the government has been doing. I defy one gentleman to stand up and say he has done it in the last ten years, and I chal lenge the Prime Minister to call into caucus or into his private office his supporters and ascertain if one of them will tell the Prime Minister that he has discharged his public duty in an endeavour to find out how public moneys have been expended, and bringing the matter to light and revealing it to the people.
If that is the case, have I made out a case for reform and for asking this particular reform to-day? I am in earnest about this matter. I have been called some uncomplimentary names in the press; at one time I was called a watch dog. Nobody likes to be called a dog. A gentleman of the Lumsden committee, that some of our friends were calling me the watch dog, but he said: I hope you do not mind, I call you the timber wolf. I did not know what' kind of an animal the timber wolf was, but I have been investigating and I am satisfied to accept the appellation. The timber wolf is not a skulker like the prairie wolf, he is all right.- But I am here to ask and I asked last session and some sessions before for some reforms in order to get the

people to know more about what is going on in the government behind this high and thick wall, in order tht the people may know what their servants are doing with their money, and I now ask that the government should concur with me in this reform, and I ask them now to allow this motion to pass without a division. If they will not, we will have a division. I therefore move:-
That the motion now read be amended by inserting therein after the figures ' 1910 ' the words and figures following, that is to say: 'and the Public Accounts and the Auditor General's Report for the year ended 31st March, 1909/

speechtext: What particular cases?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Cases in which the investigation is incomplete if confined to one year. It is our practice to
refer the public accounts of the last fiscal year to the Public Accounts Committee. If an investigation confined to the one year is incomplete, and if the House were asked to refer to the committee these accounts for a previous year, for my part I think there would be good reason to grant the request. But my hon. friend asked us to depart from a practice which has remained unchanged since confederation. He proposes that the committee should have power not only to investigate the public accounts of the last financial year, but to go over again accounts investigated the previous year. I am sure my hon. friend will see that the arguments he has used do not appeal to me. He charges that there has been dishonesty and graft, on which points I altogether disagree with him. He must not be surprised if such arguments do not impress me or other members on this side of the House. What I would suggest is that, if in the Public Accounts Committee, which is now sitting, the hon. gentleman, or any of his friends is of opinion that there is a matter which cannot be fully investigated if the investigation be confined to the accounts for one year, or that any investigation of the previous year should be reopened, that should be made a special matter; and, if the committee come to the conclusion that such a matter should be investigated, then and there it would be our duty to grant the request.	-

If the Prime Minister will allow me, he has addressed a long argument referring to cases in which there was a partial investigation of last year's public accounts and suggests that we want to go into these matters further. My argument refers to cases that do not reveal themselves before the thing has been going on for two or three years. In such a case, we begin an investigation for the first time, but we cannot complete the investigation, because we find ourselves stopped by the rules that you cannot go beyond the accounts of the financial year referred to the committee. The cases to which I refer are much more numerous than those of which the Prime Minister speaks. [DOT]

It seems to me that the hon. gentleman's argument proves too much for his amendment. [DOT] He states that it may be desired to investigate a matter that goes back two or three years. Therefore, to complete that investigation, the committee should have the accounts not merely of one previous year, but of two or three years referred to them. The hon. gentleman's amendment covers only one year. And so his argument is exactly in line with what I was pointing out. In such a case as he has indicated, it would be better to have all the accounts

involved referred to the committee that the whole transaction may be investigated. But last year's committee went through the accounts of the previous year that were referred to it. And now the hon. gentleman wants the privilege this year of going over all those accounts without exception, because that would be the effect of referring to the committee the public accounts, and the three volumes of the Auditor General's Report of the previous year. What I suggest as more reasonable is that, if it is desired to go into any of the accounts of the previous year, the matter should be brought before the committee, and if the committee recommend the investigation of accounts of previous years, that recommendation can be discussed and adopted here. For these reasons, I move, in amendment to the amendment:
That when, in a. report of the committee on public accounts, it is recommended that particular items of the Auditor General's Report of the previous year be referred to the said committee, the House will favourably consider said recommendation.

Last session this House did me the honour of placing me on the Public Acounts Committee. I do not know for what reason I was selected for that position, unless it be that I was somewhat widely known as a business man. When I attended that committee I confess that I was much disappointed at the proceedings. I supposed that I was going there practically in the capacity of a director in a concern, the concern being this great Dominion of Canada, that the shareholders were the people of this Dominion, and that the right hon. the Prime Minister was the president of this company. Sir, I found an entirely different state of affairs, I found that while our worthy chairman-against whom I have not a word to say, because I think he wishes to do what is fair and right-I found opposed to me as a layman, as a man of business training, an array of eminent lawyers, as you might call them, sitting alongside the chairman, and particularly my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley), who is known to be a lawyer. He is always very close to the ear of the chairman, and when anything comes up touching his department, he is always ready to give the wink to the gentleman who sits beside him to .plead on behalf of the government, suggesting that these gentlemen raise some legal or technical objection which the ordinary layman perhaps does not understand. Now I do not know why this government should array these gentlemen in front of the chair to raise legal and technical objections to every matter that a layman brings up. If this government are honest, if they are transacting the affairs of this country hon-Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
estly, there should toe nothing to hide My observation has alsq been directed to another state of affairs. I find that the right hon. Prime Minister and the ministers of the departments who appear in that committee, are guilty of causing some poor fellows, to perjure themselves to my mind, when they come before that committee. Perjury is not too strong a word to use in that connection. You find men coming there with an honest intention to give honest evidence, tout they are so twisted and bamboozled by objections and otherwise, that they are afraid to open their mouths. We find even civil servants coming there, whose bread and butter depend on their trying to screen any misdoing of this government or their agents. Now, Sir, I want to say that if a business man, a layman, is to be of any use at all on that committee, the Prime Minister must adopt the policy of allowing him to get at the truth from the witnesses who appear, to get at what he believes to be the truth; then I think we will find in many instances that the ordinary layman will he of some use in getting at the truth, because he will adopt common sense, business methods,and will obtain a better result than the committee are now obtaining.
I hope the right hon. gentleman will not only agree with the amendment of my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox), but that he will reform the committee along the lines I have suggested. But if the right hon. gentleman refuses to do that if he prefers that that committee be turned into a Donnybrook Fair, as I have seen it some times, then let it be known; because there are some men with fighting qualities on this side of the House and we are ready for a fight. But we would rather fight as gentlemen, we would rather do our duty to our constituents, and to our country, than to engage in these unseemly wranghngs that take place in that committee. I have had the honour of sitting as a member in another legislature than this, and sitting on the opposition benches, in the days when my hon. friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham), was a member of that legislature, and was chairman of the Public Accounts Committee; and I must say, Mr. Speaker, that "in the worst days of that committee it was very much superior to the Public Accounts Committee of this House of Commons. After the hon. gentleman vacated that position, or after he was compelled to, the committee reformed its proceedings, so that they can now go back one or two years, or even three years, if need be, and investigate any transaction that happens to be under investigation; they can investigate it from the start right up to the minute the committee is sitting. Therefore, I do not see why the amendment of my hon. friend from Simcoe, should not be accepted, unless

this government wishes to hold a club over the heads of the opposition, and prevent them from seeing what the public is entitled to see. I am sorry to see that the Prime Minister does not agree with my hon. friend from Simcoe, and I still hope that he will change his mind.

Having had some experience with this much abused Public Accounts Committee, I think it is only fair that I should offer some ob. servations on the motion which has been made, and concerning which my hon. friend who has just sat down (Mr. Smyth), has seen fit to make a speech, devoid of any arguments, that I could see, bearing upon the matter in question. If it be true that perjury is committed in that committee, if it be true, as he says, that a layman does not meet with the success which he thinks he deserves in investigating the public accounts, I cannot for the life of me, see how that state of things is going to be improved by adopting the motion of the hon. member for Simcoe, (Mr. Lennox). If there is perjury, and if there are improper proceedings, if there is unfairness to laymen in regard to the investigations of one year's accounts, evidently all that trouble will be doubled if the accounts of two years are submitted to the committee. Now I cannot understand why this motion should be made. The Committee of Public Accounts is as alert now as it has been at any time since confederation. Ever since confederation there have been member^, belonging to the opposition on that committee who have made it their business to investigate the affairs of the year as they have gone along. Is it that the present opposition is not so alert as the oppositions of past years have been? Is it that they are not so assiduous in attending to the business of the country as in past years? Up to the present time they have been able, in the year under consideration, to investigate the accounts of that year, and if they are not able to do so at the present time, surely it is a reflection upon those watch dogs, or those timber wolves, as they may style themselves, if they do not do their duty in that respect.
Now, I am glad to hear the praise of the conduct of the chairman of that committee, and I think it is well deserved. We have heard these charges of abuse with reference to the Public Accounts Committee. Surely there have been some instances which can be pointed out where the chairman has not done his duty. But, we have hon. gentlemen coming here saying in one breath, there are abuses in that committee, and in the other breath, we have them saying that we have a chairman against whom no complaint whatever can be made. These two stories do not hold together. If there are abuses
the chairman is the man to rectify them, and yet they say that the chairman's conduct has been perfectly satisfactory, and I am sure it has been. Speaking with reference to the time before that of the present chairman, the greatest complaints that I have heard have not been entirely against members on this side of the House. It must be remembered that most of the work of the committee is at the instance of members from the other side of the House. It must be remembered that members on the other side of the House mainly cross-examine the witnesses, and I have heard it said that they, too, mainly tried to distort the evidence so that the real facts are not known. I do not take much stock in that sort of thing. In every Public Accounts Committee you hear the same thing. If you read the history of the Public Accounts Committee in the great mother of parliaments, you find the same accusation made. We have it in the Public Accounts Committee here where reference is made to what has gone on in the province of Ontario, where my hon. friend the last speaker, I am sure, will agree that there is the most perfect organization to be found in any parliament. I recollect that two years ago it was brought up when something was asked to be done. It was pointed out that they had not done it in the province of Ontario under the great Whitney administration, but immediately the friends of that gentleman said: That is only a provincial organization and we cannot follow them here because we are dealing with matters on a higher plane. In so far as I know, there has been the greatest facility for investigation in the Public Accounts Committee with respect to matters brought up before that committee.
Oh, oh.

If an effort is made to go back two or three years, I think that any chairman of a committee would say that it is not within the province of the committee unless there has been a special reference to it for that purpose. I know quite well that when I had the honour of being chairman of the committee, no matter how far back the committee wanted to go, whether it wanted to go two or twenty years back, it had a perfect right to go back, so long as the inquiry had relation to the item under consideration. But when it is proposed to deal minutely with items two or three years back I think it has been invariably the ruling in this committee as well as in other committees that it is something over which the committee has no jurisdiction, because it is beyond the reference, it is beyond the matters which properly are assigned to the committee to investigate.
COMMONS [DOT]
I do not know of any case where the? fullest investigation has not been permitted with regard to the matters which have been referred to the committee. It is an easy matter, if there are other things to be investigated, to obtain a reference, and I db not understand that the Public Accounts Committee, under the general order of reference, is the only one that investigates. If there are charges of improper conduct then, quite properly, the House will refer them to that committee, or to any other committee, but the Public Accounts Committee, as I understand it, is a routine committee; it is not there to investigate scandals, it is not there to investigate charges, it is there to investigate the routine accounts of the preceding year. There is the fullest opportunity, to investigate them. If the one year's accounts cannot be investigated in one year, surely there is very little hope of having the committee properly investigate them by referring to them accounts of two years ago, especially with the growing business with which the committee has to deal. It may be said that in times past there were not so many expenditures. It is also to be said that in times past the sessions were not so long as they are to-day. The matters for investigation are greater in proportion as the length of _ the session is greater, and if we are going to leave arrears over we will never get through. It seems to me that the amendment submitted by my right, hon. friend the leader of the government (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) to complete the investigations which have not been completed must certainly meet every reasonable requirement. If, beyond that, some one discovers that in past years there has been some terrible scandal, it is perfectly open for any hon. member to bring it up in the House, and if there are sufficient grounds, it is open to the House to refer it to that committee or any other committee to investigate the charge.

Mr. Speaker, the chief reason why the rules governing the Public Accounts Committee are unsatisfactory to the opposition is beeause this government insist upon purchasing goods from middlemen. That matter was very fully discussed in the committee and in the House some two or three years ago, and it would be useless to occupy the attention of the House this afternoon with a further discussion of it except to show that the principal reason for our objection is that the government will insist upon keeping a large number of middlemen supplying goods at enormous prices. For example, one gentleman supplied goods to the government and was protected by the Public Accounts Committee. He -was de-Mr. A. H. CLARKE.
fended by the committee. After a good deal of effort on the part of the opposition we were able to bring to light the important fact that that gentleman hacl supplied some articles to the government at enormous prices, and when we made an attempt to find out how much these goods should have cost the country we were denied that right and voted down in the committee. But the opposition did not stop at that, and finally we were able to discover that Mr. Merwin had purchased an article for $756 and had sold it to the government for $1,250, making a profit of $493 on one article. What the opposition members in the Public Accounts Committee have stated and what, I believe, the people of the country will endorse is that this government should not have dealt with Merwin at all, but that the article should have been purchased by the department itself for $756 and $493 left in the treasury. That is what we are complaining about. This discussion is up this afternoon because members of the committee on the government side are in the committee not as defenders of the public treasury but as defenders of the middlemen who supply the government with goods. I could give a number of instances of the purchase of such articles, but that is not necessary because that exemplifies the methods of these middlemen who are supplying goods to this government. The attention of the government has been directed to this, we have moved a resolution in the House calling upon the government to do away with the middlemen, my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) and every member on this side has supported that resolution, the resolution was voted down in this House and the middleman prospers and flourishes under this government. I want to read the resolution that was moved in the Public Accounts Committee last year by my hon. friend from North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) :
Moved by Mr. Sharpe, and seconded by Mr. Goodeve:
That whereas one of the chief functions of the Public Accounts Committee is the investigation into all questions as to the fair and reasonable price paid by the government for the various commodities sold and services rendered to the government; and whereas to properly discharge this duty it is absolutely necessary that the greatest latitude be given to members of the committee to inquire into the first cost of such'commodities and services to the persons selling same to the government; therefore the committee deprecates the unwarranted and continual interruption, obstruction of the work of the committee by some of its members, and regrets that the rulings of the chairman, Mr. Warburton, in the present investigation before the committee prevented a full and free inquiry into all the facts of the case.

That motion was put with the following result :
Yeas: Messrs. Blain, Crosby, Currie (Sim-coe), Goodeve, Hughes, Lake, Sharpe (Ont).
Nays:	Messrs. Allen, Carvell, Congdon,
Loggie, MacNut|t, McAllister, McKenzie, Neely, Parent, Proulx, Rankin, Reid (Resti-gouche).
Voted down, seven voting for it and twelve against it. Who were w7e working for then, the public? We were working for the middlemen to be put out of business in this country, to put it plainly. My hon. friend from North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) was making a special effort to find out the first cost of heating and lighting public buildings in Ottawa.
I think the gentleman must be mistaken. There was no such resolution passed with regard to the building occupied by the Department of Labour.
I stand corrected, I intended to say the Woods Canadian building. Does the hon. minister deny that that resolution, which applies to the same thing-
It does not apply to the same thing.

After all is not the tactics now being followed by the hon. minister the very same as those followed in the Committee on Public Acoounts? My hon. friend gets up and thinks he has gained a great victory.
Not at all.

Yes, this is the kind of tactics the member uses in the Public Accounts Committee. Oh, he says, there is nothing wrong, that was not the building at all. Does he deny that we were trying to find out the first cost of heating and lighting the Woods Canadian building? He knows that to be the case, and because we are making an effort to find out why the hon. gentleman's own department and other departments in this government do not purchase these goods direct instead of through middlemen, he takes objection in the committee and in the House talso. But the hon. member cannot get away from the responsibility he owes the people when he practically tells the people that he and his colleagues will continue, notwithstanding the efforts of the opposition, to feed these middlemen and pay these enormous profits until we put this government out of office. The cost of lighting and heating was about $9,000 to the government, but the real cost, as brought out by my hon. friend from North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) was about $6,000, so that because this government did not purchase this lighting and heating direct, but through middlemen, the country lost $3,000 per year on that trans-27
action in the lighting and heating of one building only. I shall not follow this further. The hon. member for Essex (Mr. Clarke) asked me to name a case or two. Well, I can give another offhand. The Minister of Militia purchased some subtarget guns a few years ago and in that transaction the middlemen also flourished. The government gave a contract for the sum of $250 each. The company which received the contract without tender had no factory or place of business in this country at all, so they went down to Sherbrooke and bought these guns from a firm there at $64 each; and that company, without ever touching a gun, sent in a bill for $250 each, which was paid by the treasury of the country. What my hon. friend from South Simcoe is now asking is that this government will do away with these middlemen and will, when they require sub-target guns, or any other articles, purchase them direct at first cost. Then these enormous profits which for years have been paid to the middlemen, and are still being paid them, will be -saved to the people. I listened attentively to the remarks of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister. Sometimes he takes a long time to consider a question and consults his friends before -coming to a decision. At other times he does not consult them, but makes up his mind very quickly. Last year he said he would consider this question. He has given a very plausible reason why he did not, but it seems to me that when he could find so little objection to the resolution, and if his government be as honest as he tries to make us believe it is, he ought to be willing to allow the Public Accounts Committee to go back two years or more if they so desire. It is no argument to say that -such was not the custom of the past. We are supposed to make some progress, and if there were fetters around the Public Accounts Committee in this connection in the past, even if they were put there by the Conservative party, I am not going to say that they should not be removed. If the party in power be what it styles itself, a party of reform, it would consent unanimously to this resolution, and I am sure that my right hon. friend, when he takes time to consider it, will reproach himself for not having at once consented. All we ask is that, with our present rules, crippled as we are, we should have the right to go back two years in the pubic accounts if we think that necessary and investigate, not only the accounts of last year, but those of the year before.

I have listened with interest to the debate on the motion introduced by my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) regarding the powers and duties of the Public Ac-



counts Committee. What is the duty of that committee? It is to investigate the public accounts which are referred to it, in order to elucidate everything that appears in the Auditor General's Report. If, in order to do this, it be necessary, in any particular instance, to go back to the preceding year or the preceding two years, you reouire no order from this House to do that. That power is in the Public Accounts Committee to-day, as the hon. member for Essex (Mr. Clarke) intimates. If, for the purpose of clearing up any expenditure, it be necessary to go back two or three years into the public accounts, the committee does not require to come to this House to get the authority to do that. The investigations of the committee should be confined to the accounts of the year, but if there be in the public accounts an expenditure which has continued some four or five years, there is nothing to prevent the committee from deciding to go back four or five years in order to inquire into that expenditure. That is within the power of the committee and it need not come to this House.
But they do not do that.

That is for the chairman to decide. If he makes a ruling that the committee cannot go back beyond the present year, he is unduly limiting the power of the committee. The power to refer back to previous years is one that was always exercised by the committee in my time, and is a power vested in the committee, as the hon. member for Essex (Mr. Clarke) has pointed out. But these transactions of previous years must be pertinent to the accounts referred to the committee this year, otherwise you have no right to inquire into them. Why should it be necessary to adopt an amendment such as the one before us? I was in the Public Accounts Committee when a motion was made for the purpose of appealing from that committee to this House and it was carried. You would think that such a motion would be sent at once to this House and the power required obtained for the purpose of making a full inquiry. But how did they block it? They did not report it. They simply said that the account had not been fully inquired into and there is no report to send to the House. But what is most annoying and objectionable to one who has been m the House, as I have been, for nearly forty years, is the course followed in the Public Accounts Committee in the questioning of witnesses., which my hon. friend has described. That course would be a disgrace to the lowest police court in any portion of the country. The rule governing these committees is that you are not limited by any legal rules as to the questions you put to a witness; but when a question is asked, two or three lawyers on the committee bob up and raise the ' Mr. J. HAGGART.
legal point that it is not a right or proper one. The question is on the authority of the man asking the question. Is it pertinent to the inquiry? If it is, there is no limitation by any legal rule. The committee is a farce. A matter may be referred to that committee and it cannot be inquired into, because the moment we commence questioning, some legal objection is raiseu. It is referred to the chairman. You appeal from the chairman's ruling to this House; but the question is not referred to the House until there is a general report of the committee on the question. It is time a stop were put to the manner of conducting the committees of this House. The Public Accounts Committee particularly is a disgrace to the country. The minister who should take the most intense interest in a matter of inquiry, and, if there is anything wrong, should assist the opposition in exposing it, acts as if there were something which would not bear the light, and assists his friends in the committee to defeat inquiry

Mr. Speaker, I would not have deemed it my duty to intervene in this discussion had it not been that references have been made to a ruling which I made in the Public Accounts Committee last year, a ruling for which I take absolute and full responsibility, which I thought then and still think was right. It came up on a motion that the ruling of the Chair be. not sustained. The last speaker could not have attended the meetings of the Public Accounts Committee last session, or he would have known that the charge he made, that members of the committee were not allowed to ask questions because they were interrupted by lawyers, and because the Chair sustained the objections of these lawyers, was not borne out by the facts. There was scarcely a question submitted during all the meetings of the Public Accounts Committee last session, of which I had the honour to be the chairman, as I am now, which I did not allow to be put, although exception was repeatedly taken by members supporting the government.	-
I may say to the hon. gentleman that I was not in the committee last session, and his ruling may have been an exception.

The hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) last year took exception to questions being asked, and had I been sitting as a judge in a court of law, I unquestionably would have sustained his objection. But I laid down this principle, that in my view the committee was not a court of law, but a committee of inquiry, two-thirds of the members oi which were not lawyers, and could not be

expected to understand the technical rules of evidence, and therefore they ought to " be allowed considerably more latitude than would be allowed in a court of law. I may be right or wrong, but that was the principle on which I acted throughout the whole of last session; but I did not propose to allow that latitude to become license. With respect to my ruling with regard to the Woods building, which has been referred to, the facts of that ruling have not been stated to the House. It seems that in 1897, speaking from memory. Mr. Woods had erected a buildiing which is now rented by the government. I think it is known as the Woods building. He had at the same time a manufacturing industry in the city of Ottawa. He had made a contract with the Electric Consumers' Company to supply him with light and power at a certain flat rate. It was evidently a very low rate, which was easily to be gathered from the evidence before the committee. The reason for that flat rate subsequently came out. We had evidence from the manager of the Municipal Electric Company, and he was asked whether that flat rate was not a very low one. I did not allow evidence to be given as to what the original flat rate was, but the evidence of the manager was that they would not give that flat rate now, and they had given it at the time the original contract was made only because the company had a large surplus of power which they were prepared to give at a very low rate. The matter was investigated at great length before the Public Accounts Committee. Later on Mr. Woods, or the Woods Company, erected the building known as the Canadian building, and carried on negotiations with the Consumers' Company to obtain light and power at the same flat rate as they had got previously, and the company verbally agreed that they would give Mr. Woods or his company the same rate for the new building that -they had given for the old. The contract was not actually reduced to black and white when the city took over the Consumers' Company's plant and work, but it had been carried to that extent that the city considered that they should carry out the contract. They had taken over the Consumer's lighting plant and electrical plant with the undertaking that they were to assume and carry out all the agreements and contracts entered into by that company, and although this agreement had not been actually reduced to legal form they considered, nevertheless as, it had been really negotiated, and the negotiations completed that they should carry it out and they did so. We thus have the same terms for the new building that they had for the old. When the government rented from them this building they entered into
a contract with Mr. Woods or the Imperial Company to supply light and power at the ordinary rate for supplying light and power, that has come out in evidence, and a contract to that effect was entered into by the Department of Public Works. That contract was allowed to go before the committee without objection, but the gentleman who was conducting the investigation wanted to go further and find out the business contract between the old Consumers' Company and Mr. Woods, now represented by the Imperial Company. His general manager objected and said that it was exposing their private business to the public, because this was a contract made before the government had anything to do with the matter, and even although they had a good contract, and a good arrangement, that was no business of the public, or of the committee, or of the government. I sustained them in that objection, and I thought at the time I was doing right, I think so still. Repeated efforts were made to bring in that old agreement, and I invariably ruled against them, and if such a thing should happen during the present session and a precisely similar case should come before me, I should rule the same way. I do not think it is a fair thing for a private company to bring out an agreement of this kind made between them and a private company before the government had anything to do with it.
Not even in the public interests.	[DOT]

I do not think it is in the public interest to unnecessarily interfere with a private individual, but there was no difficulty in the way of the opposition or any one else ascertaining whether or not the government paid too much for light and power. They could have summoned the managers of the local electric companies or any large consumer of electricity in this city without going into private contracts made years before with individuals.
Was not Mr. Linton who represented the company quite willing to supply the contract for use in the committee, only my hon. friend the chairman said he should not be compelled to do so.

No, I would say that Mr. Linton did object. He said he would obey the orders of the Chair, but he objected to supplying it. Through an error of my own I ordered that he should give up the contract or agreement which I at the moment thought was the one between the government and the Imperial Company, but it turned out to be the old contract to the production of which there had been objection. When it was called to my attention that the wrong paper had been handed oyer I insisted on its being returned.

As a member of the Public Accounts Committee for many years I wish to corroborate the statements of my hon. friend from Peel. I moved for papers a few years ago in reference to purchases made by the Public Works Department in Montreal from Mr. Lymburner. The hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes) handled the matter before the Public Accounts Committee and it was proved to the satisfaction of the minister himself that they had overpaid, and he said he would have the man who certified the accounts properly dealt with and would let us know later but we have never heard of it since. Lymburner sold to the government leather belting at list prices, thousands of dollars worth, whereas every manufacturer in the House will bear me out in saying that any manufacturer could have bought the same goods not at the list price but at 60 and 10 and 10 and 10 off and could buy it to-day for that. I made a contract only a few days ago for a quantity for our factory at 60 and 10 and 10 and 10 off. The government paid %, dollar for what a private individual would pay 29 cents. The Minister of Public Works was to have a stop put to that sort of thing. But what do we find in the Auditor General's Report to-day? The same purchasing from the same Lymburner of thousands of dollars worth, at nearly every page in the Auditor General's Report, purchases from this man who took out of the public money of this country 601 cents on every dollar's worth purchased after we had x>roved to the satisfaction of the Minister of Public Works in the Public Works Department that this overcharge was being made. Yet this same fellow is now taking his rake-off, no doubt handing back to the government a portion of it because they would not let any man steal that much and put it in his own pocket. It is currently reported in the country that these men would get the rake-off, hand over 20 per cent of their rake-off to go into a campaign fund. I have had this statement made to me by some of the men who are selling to the government. We want that kind of thing stopped, we want the honest money of the people spent honestly, not giving 604 cents on every dollar to some middleman for his benefit or for the benefit of the party to which he may belong. It is for that purpose that we are asking the Prime Minister to see that the Public Accounts Committee is properly conducted. Hon. gentlemen opposite should be as anxious as we are to know that the people's money is spent properly, and they should aid in these investigations. The Minister of Public Works promised that in the case of leather belting, that would stop and there would not be any more purchasing from Lymburner. At page 0-96 of the Auditor General's Report there is a purchase from Lymburner of $2,785. At V in Mr. WARBURTON.
the minister's own department, Lymburner is down for $152 in one place.
I thought the hon. gentleman said that thousands and thousands of dollars worth were purchased from Lymburner for my department.
I said the hon. tleman said that thousands and thousands of dollars worth of leather belting.

The hon. gentleman said in the first place that we bought thousands at a charge of upwards of a dollar and we had continued to buy thousands of dollars worth from Lymburner at the same outrageous prices.

I am charging the government, my hon. friend is not the government. At page O-96 Lymburner is dow'n for $2,785. I have only glanced at the Auditor General's Report, I may find it at every page. How much of that $2,785, on which there is a rake-off of 70} cents on every dollar, went to the campaign fund? My hon. friend said there would be no more purchasing of this kind but it is going on and who is getting the rake-off? We want to know that the people's money is spent properly and it cannot be when the government ask for such an outrageous sum as one hundred and thirty odd million dollars, where we used to run the country, years ago, practically as well as it is run now. with $40,000,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Is this charged in the last report of the Auditor General?

Yes, the report now before us. And the government are responsible, because the Minister of Public Works said that the man that certified to that account said that he could have bought for 29} cents what the government paid $1 for
What department?

The Public Works Department-bought for the custom-house at Montreal. My hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes) can tell more about that, because he handled the witnesses in the case. We should know this session how many thousand the government have bought, and if the rake-off is as much as one would suppose it to be. From the price charged the total rake-off will be pretty large. But we will investigate the matter.
I am sure the House will agree that if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) gets as excited in the Committee on Public Accounts as he is here
I am not excited.

Then, if the hon. gen-} tleman, when he is not excited, talks in the same way before the committee as in this House, one can see how quickly trouble would arise in that committee. I have observed, in the comparatively few times that I have had the opportunity of attending upon the Public Accounts Committee, that lion, gentlemen on the other side who are members of that committee are very apt to ask questions which they know are entirely inadmissible and to seek to go into matters which are entirely irrelevant to the question before the committee.
Would the minister give us one case of an irrelevant question being asked?

I could give many, though I may not have particulars before me at the moment. These hon. gentlemen are very apt to ask mere hearsay questions. I have known such cases; and the chairman, in the fair discharge of his duty, has refused to allow them to bring out evidence of that character on the ground that the proper evidence is the original evidence, documentary or otherwise, Hon. gentlemen opposite have complained very bitterly that they were not allowed to bring out hearsay evidence. I have in mind a case which occurred last session. One of the hon. gentlemen who have spoken said I had been an offender before the Committee on Public Accounts and had given the wink to certain members-that I was close to the chairman
Many a time.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Smyth), even though he ransacks his memory, will fail to produce a single case in which I acted in that way before the committee. I appeal to hon. gentlemen who are members of that committee, I appeal to the chairman, if I have, directly or indirectly, tried to influence him in the judgment he gives as head of that committee. How inconsistent are these hon. gentlemen opposite. In one breath they declare that we have an excellent chairman, one with whom they have no fault to find; and in the next breath, they insinuate that the chairman is influenced by suggestions made by myself as a member of the committee and a member of the government. They must have but little regard for the chairman if they desire this House to believe that he would be influenced by any intimation which a member of the government might give.
I differ entirely from some hon. gentlemen on the other side who have spoken as to the conduct of the Committee on Public Accounts. So far as I have observed,
there has been every disposition to investigate the accounts as appearing in thei Auditor General's Report, in the fullest and freest manner. Speaking of all that I have seen of that committee since I entered this parliament, every opportunity! has been given for the fullest investigation. But when hon. members ask questions which they know to be improper, there is nothing for the chairman to do but to rule out those questions. I believe these gentlemen ask such questions simply in order to be prevented from putting them, that they may have a grievance, something which may appear in the newspapers to show that, in some way, they are denied the opportunity to expose the public business before the country. My hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Taylor) says that what the mover of this resolution desires is to prevent the government purchasing from middlemen. Surely the mover, my hon. friend from South Simeoe (Mr. Lennox) has taken a queer way to accomplish that end. That would be a proper subject of a substantive resolution before the House, but he has not moved such a resolution.
With the permission of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley)-such a resolution was moved in this House and voted down by the minister and his friends on that side.

It is just possible that the motion referred to may have been a want of confidence motion, or may have been moved at an improper time. I am not aware that in the Department of Public Works there is any middleman, nor am I aware that middlemen supply goods to other departments.
How about the sawdust wharf?

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Blain), must have a strange idea of the meaning of words when he suggests that the man who sold the so-called sawdust wharf was a middleman. He was not; he was the owner of the property. And, so far as I know, neither he nor anybody else, got a rake-off. He received what a great many people said was the fair value of the property, and no man from the county of Kent or from the town of Richi-bucto', except the political partisan, who came here to give evidence against the government
How many days, may I ask, had he owned the sawdust wharf?

A good many weeks -several months. We tried all that out: and I repeat that no middleman or anybody else received a rake-off. so far a? I know. The government paid for the

property what many people swore was its fair value, and what no disinterested man from Richibucto or elsewhere in New Brunswick could be induced to testify was anything but a reasonable price. But, as a matter of fact, how will this resolution effect the purpose which the hon. member for Leeds and others say is to 'be effected?
Mr: LENNOX. Will the hon. gentleman like me to tell him?
Yes.

Suppose a government work was begun two years and a half ago. At first, things go on very nicely. After a while, one year's accounts come in. There is nothing there to challenge public attention or to put the opposition on the alert. But the second year's accounts came in, as they came in the other day. Perhaps we find window blinds or curtains charged up, and we suppose that the goods bought are window blinds er curtains. But suppose it is found that they are not window blinds or curtains, but ladies' dresses,-"we want to investigate that account, and go not only over the last year's accounts, but over the accounts of the year before. But we are not permitted to do that. If my resolution carries, we shall be permitted to do it. And I want it for that reason. I want it also because it will remove the temptation to the blocking which goes on in that committee. As long as hon. gentlemen opposite know that by staving us off from one year they will stave us off altogether, they will do their blocking, as the minister has helped them to do. But, with this resolution passed, that kind of thing would be curtailed.
My hon. friend, I am sure, is not serious, when he says that I ever helped to block the committee.

Does the minister forget the sub-target gun case where a lawyer of the government party was chairman and where prominent lawyers of the government party were engaged in the matter, where a minister was assisting, and two other ministers of the Crown were assisting as well? It was about as glaring a ease, as barefaced a case of blocking, as ever occurred in a committee.

I can tell my hon. friend that he is entirely mistaken. I have a very good memory, and I know my hon. friend is just as wrong as the hon. member for Peel was, when he said that there was an investigation last year into the lighting of the building occupied by the Minister of Labour; my hon. friend from Sim-coe is just as much in error in what he says. So far as I recollect, I had nothing in the world to do with the investigation of the gun target case.
My recollection is otherwise.

I do not remember being present during the investigation. Now just a word w'ith reference to this motion. My hon. friend from Simcoe says that he wants _ to carry the investigation further back in respect of accounts which appear in the Auditor General's Report actually before the committee. Now it seems to. me that my hon. friend from South Lanark, has answered the hon. member as to that, because he says that where the committee is engaged in investigating an account they have a perfect right to turn back to the Auditor General's Report of the previous years. But if the amendment of the Prime Minister is adopted, there will be no question' about this House, when asked, always giving to the committee an opportunity to go back and trace an account to the previous year, and I have no doubt that upon their request they would be allowed to go back even beyond the previous year. But what I object to, and what I understood the Prime Minister to object to, is that, upon a motion of my hon. friend, the Auditor General's Reports of previous years are to go holus bolus before the Committee on Public Accounts, which may thus have a right to begin an original investigation into accounts which may not appear at all in the Auditor General's Report for the last preceding year, but which may appear in the report of the previous year. If my hon. friend's amendment is to prevail, they would have a right to investigate accounts of the previous year which do not "appear at all in the Auditor General's Report for the last preceding year. My hon. friend I think will agree with me.
I agree with the minister, if he will allow me a word.
Yes.

I do not care whether they occur in the last year's financial report or not, they may or they may not. But I say that within the limit of two years, this auditing body should have the right to take upon themselves to say what accounts they will investigate; and as long as they do not go back more than two years, they may take into the Public Accounts Committee whatever they think is best in the public interest. That is all I claim.

My hon. friend is getting away from what he first gave as his reason for the motion. The reason he first gave wras that the committee should have the right to investigate accounts in the Auditor General's Report, which were running back to the preceding year, when they might find it desirable to go back. Now he says that he wants the accounts for both years referred to them, accounts which

might run into each other, to investigate the accounts of .two years ago as well as the accounts of the last year. Now, Sir, that would be unsatisfactory. The effect would be that instead of making the committee diligent in doing their work during the present session, they might feel inclined to let a case stand over this year with the intention of taking it up next year. If they were inclined to neglect their business they might leave an account open to the next year, with the privilege of going into accounts which they had entirely neglected during the current year.

I understand the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) to say that the Public Works Department was paying $1 per foot for leather belting, and he added that he or any other manufacturer could buy it in the market for 29J cents a foot. That statement was proved in the Public Accounts Committee. What has the minister to say to that?

No, that is not correct. The hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor)
I regret has only told half the story with regard to that belting; I will give the other half. Instead of it being an account for many thousands of dollars, it was an account, if I remember rightly, of some $400 or $500, and probably even less than that. It appears that the account included labour, included installing the belting, and included a great deal of night work. The man was called upon suddenly to install this belting, and my recollection is that all the services and the labour in connection with it were added to the price of the belting. I do not profess to have all the facts in mind at the present time, but I am safe in saying that instead of the account being for thousands, it was only for a very few hundreds.

I did not state that he paid $1 a foot. I stated that he bought it at list prices, on which any manufacturer could buy it at 60, 10 and 10 off. Then I illustrated by a dollar's worth. 1 did not say what the price was.

My hon. friend is quoting the manufacturer's price. This was a small quantity of belting which Mr. Lymburner was buying. He was not a manufacturer or a wholesale dealer. None but a wholesale dealer could buy it at that price.
Any manufacturer could buy it at that.

This was not a manufacturer. My hon. friend knows perfectly well that an employee of the government requiring to get a small quantity of belting could hot get it at the manufacturer's price. These discounts are only given to
wholesale purchasers; my hon. friend from South Lanark knows that.
You can go into any hardware store and buy belting on these conditions.

Then my hon. friend ought to explain to the House why the manufacturer has different prices, and what these discounts mean which are deducted from the original price. As I understand it, the belting was bought at the ordinary list price, but the labour was included in it.
Mr. TAYLOR (Leeds) No, no.
I think so.
He charged for labour separately.

My hon. friend will have an opportunity before the Committee of Public Accounts to investigate any purchases which may have been made by Mr. Lymburner, fust as he had the fullest opportunity to investigate those of a few years ago. But what I rose to say is that I do not think my hon. friend from Simcoe should press his amendment, which would have the effect of throwing holus bolus before the committee the accounts of both years. There ought to be a limit fixed, so that only upon a request of the committee may the accounts of preceding years be investigated. in which case the committee would make the request to the House, and if the amendment of the Prime Minister is carried the House will accede to that request and allow the committee to carry its investigations back as far as necessary, not only to the preceding year, but back even beyond that, in order to get the information they might desire.

The Minister of Public Works started out by reprimanding my hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Taylor) because he appeared to be excited. Well, when one comes to read these transactions before the Public Accounts Committee he is liable to get excited, because of their extraordinary character. The dishonesty and unfairness of the proceedings of the committee are enqugh to make any one feel indignant. When they are refused the opportunity of bringing it out it is an additional reason why they should feel somewhat indignant. I cannot return the compliment to the Minister of Public Works, because I have noticed that very frequently when he gets up in his place to defend a transaction which is somewhat off colour-he may get up one time or twenty times-he is as calm, serene, bland and innocent looking as any pirate that ever scuttled a ship or cut a throat. There is no excitement-not

at all. He disarms criticism by the very innocent appearance that he always displays, especially if his case is very bad.
Long practice.

Yes, long practice. I was amused at the reasons given by the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) for the refusal to allow this motion to pass. What were they? The first one was that we are in the middle of a parliament and this is not the time to reform committee work ; the proper time is at the beginning of a new parliament ; let it go now, we will leave the question over for a while and then at the commencement of - the next parliament we can reform parliament as we choose. That suggests the old proverb about locking the stable after the horse is stolen. That is just what this is. They are stealing the horses right and left and we do not want the stable door to be left open until they are all stolen. I do not think the country will regard that as a very strong reason why this motion should be rejected. What is the next reason? The House will consider any case that is sent from the committee to the House desiring the right to go back. But the supporters of the government will not allow the committee to report a case to the House to get the right. Then, how are they to get it? Time after time they have been refused that right when they desired to make a report so as to get further powers from the House delegated to them. They are absolutely denied that right, therefore, they cannot do it and I have no doubt that the same course will be pursued in the future as that which has been pursued in the past. Another hon. member says : Well but the committee is willing to report at any time and the House is willing to consider it. The committee may be willing to report, but the members of the committee who are doing the work cannot get an opportunity of reporting so that the House has not an opportunity of inquiring into the matter or of giving further instructions to the committee.
I	was a member of that committee for many years, but two years ago I asked to be relieved of the work and to be transferred to some other committee. Why? For the simple reason that I went there year after year, and if I desired to do what I would do in connection with any private business transaction, commercial or otherwise, in regard to which I was endeavouring to ascertain whether money had been properly expended or not, that is to bring out the information, what happened? I ask a question according to my way of bringing out the information and the question is scarcely propounded before some lawyer jumps up and says : I Mr. SPROULE
object to that ; it would not be allowed in any court of law ; that is not according to the rules of evidence. You may remind that gentleman, as we did many times over, that we are not governed by the rules .of evidence, that we have the right to ask any question we desire so long as it bears on the subject and is likely to bring out the information, but we are badgered from minute to minute and from hour to hour with the result that the whole time of the committee is absolutely frittered away. You cannot do the work in the same way as it would be done by any private commercial concern, or by a board of directors, when you undertake to look into the expenditure of public money. This kind of thing takes place over and over again until the layman is almost afraid to attempt to ask a question in the committee in the performance of the duty for which he is sent here. The result is that in the performance of that part of his parliamentary duties his efforts are paralysed by the conduct of what is termed, outside of this House, the blockers brigade, because we found that they would not allow us to go on with the work. It had become so disagreeable, so unpleasant, so offensive that many laymen have left the committee and will not attempt to do any work upon it. I asked to be relieved of membership in that committee and to be transferred to some other committee because I thought that my time could be used to better advantage elsewhere. I found that I could do nothing on account of the way that we were obstructed. Sometimes it is done by a minister of the Crown, or by friendly lawyers who are always there ready to pounce down on a member and to say :* Stop, you are a layman and do not know anything about it i you are wasting the time of the committee ; you are not following the rules of evidence. The result is that the committee is paralysed in its work. Then, the right hon. leader of the government says that they cannot get over two Auditor General's Reports. He says that the Auditor General's Report contains an expenditure of $135,000,000 or $136,000,000 and he asks : How are they going to look through an expenditure of twice that amount if they take two years? If they were allowed to conduct the investigation, as any public corporation, or any commercial concern would do, they could get through two years' expenditure with much less trouble and in a very much shorter time than they are able to do it now, in examining a portion of the expenditure of one year according to the system that has been carried out for several years past. But they are not allowed to do it and if it is to be the same in the future as it has been in the past it will not increase the work very much to take two years instead of one.

But, we are told, it has not been the custom and it is not the proper thing to do.
I	would like to ask the leader of the government if he remembers the long inquiry that took place in 1891 or 1892-I forget the exact year-in that committee with reference to the Interior Department. When it was found that some of these cases went back more than one year a request was made to this House that the public accounts of other years be referred to the committee and that they should be permitted to go back a year. The question was asked: Whv should you not go back as many years as vou like if you think there is anything wrong?-and they were allowed to go back as many years as they desired. That was the proper, the correct, the sound principle and it is one which should be followed out to-day. The very reverse is the case and at this very moment, although we believe, from the information in our possession, that we should, in the interest of the country. go back another year in many of these examinations, we are being denied the right to do that and the very high authority of the Prime Minister himself supports an amendment to this motion to deprive that committee of the right that it should have of suing back on these transactions so as to bring out the information that would protect the country's money and insure its being expended in a proper way. I think that he should be the last in the House to do that. He has not lived up to the very line of policy that he, away back in 1891 and 1892. advocated when he defended the principle that it was a right thing to go back, a principle that he does not defend to-day, and I think it is well that the attention of the country should be drawn to this featur* of it because the work of the committee is paralysed by the practice that has obtained in the committee for several years past. If this practice is continued in the future and we are prevented from bringing out the information the Public Accounts Committee is of vety little use to the country.
M- S. SHARPE (Ontario). Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention to interpose in this debate, but I listened, to the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) state that the fullest opportunity was given for investigation and that he was the last man in the world that would interrupt, or interfere with or interpose, or in any way take part in the work of obstruction in the Public Accounts Committee, and I could not allow that statement to go without calling the attention of the House to some facts that transpired in the Public Accounts Committee last year. I submit that the opposition was interfered with in a recent investigation that took place in the Public Accounts Committee by reason of the attitude and the tactics of government supporters. The Minister of Public Works was the most flagrant
sinner in that regard in the committee. He had to be repeatedly rebuked by members of the opposition, and I desire to submit to the House a few observations that were made. I am quoting from the minutes of the Public Accounts Committee. I was asking the question:
Now, I want to ask this question.
The witness was Mr. Linton, secretary of the Imperial Realty Company, and we were desirous of getting at the original contract to see what this imperial Realty Company was paying for the lighting of this building. The Imperial Realty Company had nothing to do with the manufacture of electric light, yet strange to say the government were paying that company for lighting the building, and were paying it some $6,000 a year more than the company was paying the city for that same light.
Where does that appear?
I challenge the hon. minister to produce all the papers, and he will see where it appears.
All the papers were submitted to the Committee on Public Accounts, and so far as I remember, that does not appear in any of them.

I was present and conducted the whole investigation, and I tell the hon. minister and the House that all the papers were not submitted to the committee, as will appear by the very words which I purpose reading out of the minutes of the committee:
Now, I want to ask this question and if you object to it, you can say so. Was that contract-referring to the original contract- at a meter rate or a flat rate?

The contract will speak for itself. The witness has already declined to answer that question.
Then the witness, taking his cue from the Minister of Public Works, said:
I decline to answer that question.
That is a perfectly proper question.
No, it is not?
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: What contract are you asking about now?
About the original contract. The minister says it is a fair and reasonable one so far as the government is concerned.
Which contract are you asking about? Are you asking about the contract between Mr. Woods and the government.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: You can ask about the contract between Mr. Woods and the government.

I do not think it is the per-rogative of a minister of the Crown any more

than any other member of the committee to stand between the witness and the examining counsel.
Not at all.
My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works is here apparently defending and protecting the witness.
Not at all.

I strongly object and protest against his conduct in this committee this afternoon. I say the Minister of Public Works has no right to tell a witness that he must decline to answer or to say ' you need not answer that question, or that is not a proper question.'
Mr: PUGSLEY. I am here as a member of this committee, and I have the same rights as Mr. Boyce or any other member.
A little further on I find that the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) had to rebuke the hon. Minister of Public Works for continually interrupting the witness and giving the witness a cue, so that he might refuse to answer.
The hon. minister has begged the whole question.
In what way?
Because you are presupposing that you know this witness is going to say he will not answer the question.
Not at all.

Excuse me, now, by your interjection you are intimating to the witness that he need not answer, before you know whether he will object or not. . .
The Minister of Public Works, by taking the stand that he does, is taking the stand that he is the private solicitor for the gentleman who is in the box.
How absurd.
He is, because supposing after you had made this objection the witness says: 'I do not mind answering it at all.'
That is not proper evidence.
