Then you have no right to interject your objections until you know whether the witness objects to answer or not. You are taking the position of counsel for this witness.
And to-day, we have the extraordinary spectacle of the Minister of Public Works, on the floor of this House saying that he never objected.

Will my hon. friend let me ask him a question, and I ask it of him as a lawyer-because he is a lawyer and a good one-was he not seeking to give secondary evidence of the contents of a contract that had been ruled out by the chairman of the committee?
The objection of the hon. minister
Could my hon. friend not say * yes ' or ' no ' ?

The Minister of Public Works objected to the production of Mr. SHARPE (Ontario).
the original contract because he said it was a private document.
No, I was not present when the chairman ruled out that contract.

The Minister of Public Works, and all his cohorts surrounding him, objected to the production of the original contract, because it would disclose the amount this company was paying the city of Ottawa for its light.
I have made the statement that I was not present in the committee when objection was taken to the original contract, and when it was ruled out.
I will show the minister, from the minutes of the Public Accounts Committee, when he was present:
I have always understood that the desire of the committee and government was to get at the full facts, that is my understanding, of the object of this committee.
But not to indulge the curi" osity to pry into the private affairs of the people.

I desire to repeat-and my hon. friend must either accept my statement, or give evidence to the contrary -that when the question as to the admissibility of the original contract came up, I was not present in the committee, and I was not present when the chairman ruled it out, but afterwards I appeared on another day.
And repeated the objection.

But my hon. friend, notwithstanding the original contract had been ruled out, sought to give secondary 'evidence of its contents. That is what I objected to^ and that is what the minutes show I objected to. As a lawyer, my hon. friend must admit I was perfectly aright.
The Minister of Public Works upholds the chairman. I quote again:
The chairman holds, and I think properly so, that any member of the committee has the right, if an improper question is asked, to call attention to the fact that it is an improper question.

And the minister overrules the chairman. That is just contrary to what the chairman has said.
The evidence shows conclusively and repeatedly that the Minister of Public Works repeatedly objected to the admissibility of this evidence and suggested to the witness that he should not reply. What the committee desired was the production of the original contract between the Imperial Realty Company and the city of Ottawa in order to ascertain what that company was

paying for electric light. In this instance the middleman was the Imperial Realty Company, and I challenge the Minister of Public Works to lay the documents before the House. If he does the House will ascertain that the rake-off to the company was at least $6,000 per year. In view of the evidence as printed in the minutes of the Public Accounts Committee, it ill becomes the Minister of Public Works to say that every opportunity was given the committee to investigate into all these facts, and it ill becomes him to say here that he never objected or tried to suppress the facts. The government succeeded, by reason of the ruling of the chairman, in suppressing that particular contract, but we were successful, nevertheless, in getting around that ruling by summoning the ex-mayor of Ottawa, Mr. Ellis, who was secretary of the Ottawa municipal electric plant, and the committee found out from him that the government was paying $4,425 per year at least over and above what it would have had to pay had it contracted direct with the city of Ottawa. This is set out in a resolution moved by myself. The facts were so conclusive that the deputy Minister of Public Works, and the chief architect of that department admitted that the contract was contrary to the interests of the public; and now notwithstanding the violent opposition of the hon. the Minister of Public Works and all the Liberal members of the committee, the fact was brought out that there was an annual rake-off of $4,000 or $5,000 a year for the electric lighting of these two buildings. Then we moved this resolution, which was actually seconded by Mr. Carvell, one of the principal Liberal members of that committee :
That whereas the expense to the government during the last year for lighting the Woods and! Canadian buildings amounted to $9,465.91, paid to the Imperial Realty Company, which company -is not an electrical lighting company; and whereas the city of Ottawa has a standard schedule of prices whereby the lighting would cost only $5,040 or less, thereby effecting an annual saving to the country of $4,425.91 or more; therefore this committee desires to urge upon the Minister of Public Works and the govern meat the desirability of cancelling the present arrangement and recovering the excess unjustly paid to the Imperial Realty Company, and giving the city of Ottawa or some other company the contract at lower rates; and that a copy of this resolution he forwarded to the Minister of Public Works.
From an answer to a question which I put on the Order Paper yesterday, I find that the Minister of Public Works cancelled that electric light contract, and is thereby going to save the country $3,000 or $4,000 a year; and if that evidence had been suppressed, which the Minister of Public Works and the Liberal members of the
committee were desirous of suppressing, that saving would never have been effected.
Perhaps the hon. gentleman will read the whole of my answer.

I have no objection to the hon. minister reading it if he wishes to do so. The facts are there, substantially admitted by himself. Another matter that was investigated was the heating of the building. That was actually let out to the Imperial Realty Company, which was making a rake-off of some $3,000 a year in connection with that. That contract, I understand, has also been cancelled, and the country is going to save $3,000 a year in consequence thereof, which would not have been effected if the Minister of Public Works and the Liberal members of the committee had had their way in suppressing the evidence.
A word with reference to the chairman of. the committee. The hon. gentleman who occupies that position is a most estimable gentleman, and I have not a word to say against his personal character; but I do say that he has been too easily influenced by the Minister of Public Works and the Liberal members of the committee. It required only a nod or a suggestion from the Minister of Public Works or the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell), to have any question ruled out by the chairman; and the only objection I have to the hon. gentleman is, that he is too easily influenced to suppress evidence which is in the interest of the country. The investigations before the Public Accounts Committee have amounted to a public scandal. They have been made party affairs, in which the Liberal party have again demonstrated their ability to go back on their old principle, enunciated in the Liberal platform of 1893, that it was the undoubted prerogative of the people's representatives to thoroughly investigate every expenditure of public money. That is another plank in their platform which has gone to the winds. Instead of allowing us to thoroughly investigate every expenditure, the Public Accounts Committee is organized for the purpose of obstructing investigation. The true function of a public accounts committee is to ascertain whether a price is reasonable and just to the government; and how can we ascertain that, unless we ascertain what the middleman is paving, and thereby the amount of rake-off he receives in each instance? I will support the amendment, as I believe it to be in the public interst.

(Cumberland), Mr. Speaker, I would not have said anything this afternoon, had it not been for the fact that the question of the purchase of leather belting from Lymburner, Limited, has arisen in the discussion; and, as I

conducted the proceedings in the Public Accounts Committee on that matter, J think it proper that the facts should appeal correctly on the record. The lion. Minister of Public Works said that the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. George Taylor), only told half the truth in respect to the proceedings before the committee. I have taken the trouble to get the report of the committee, and I would like to read a few words from the evidence with respect to this purchase in 1908. I may say by the way of preface, that the government purchased this leather belting, not from a leather belting manufacturer, nor from . the representative of one, but from people in Montreal, who had no connection whatever with the manufacture or sale of leather belting. The transaction arose in connection with the purchase by the Department of Public Works of four pieces of leather belting aggregating 388 feet, 7 inches in length. This is the evidence of Mr Moody, the traveller for the manufacturer of leather belting:
Q. Now, taking the total invoice prices of these four different items of leather belting at $024.09, just figure what that would come to, taking off first 60 per cent, then 10 per cent, then 10 per cent, and then 2 per cent. Perhaps you had better verify my figures, Mr. Moody?-A. I make it $293.41.
Q. You have made a computation?-A. Yes.
Q. And the sale price of these four invoices of belting, taking off the jobbers' discount, what does the same come to?-A. I made that $293.41.
Q. $293.41 ?-A. $293.41.
Q. As contrasted with $861.38 which was paid by the government?-A. Yes.
Q. The difference then would be $538.27?- A. Yes.
Q. In other words, the government by paying for this belting on the basis of a discount of 10 per cent paid $538.27 more than they could have bought it for had they purchased it at the jobbers' discounts?-A. Yes.
Q. And you would have sold-you have already stated, I think, that you would have sold the same belting to the government at the jobbers' discounts?-A. We would have.
Q. In other words you would have sold the same belting to the government for the sum of $293.41?-A. We would have.
Does my hon. friend remember what he stated the retail price was?
He stated that he would sell it to the government at the jobbers' discounts.
What would the jobbers' price be? That would be the retail price.
The retail price less., 60 and 10, and 10 and 2 per cent.

My hon. friend misunderstands me surely." The manufacturer sells to the jobber, and the jobber sells to the retailer, who sells to the ordinary pub-Mr. RHODES.
lie. Does the evidence show at what price that would be?

The evidence shows that the government bought four pieces of leather belting, for which it paid the sum of $861.38, and that this belting manufacturer's agent swore, that he would have sold the same belting to the government for the sum of $293.41; in other .words, that upon a transaction involving to this government a total cost of $861.38 there was a rake-off pure and simple of $538.27. There is not much dispute about that evidence, it was verified, it was amplified by the evidence of other leather belting manufacturers. in fact was so strong that the hon. member for Carleton, New Brunswick, (Mr. Carvell), at the close of the proceedings, rose and made these remarks and I would like to have them embalmed in ' Hansard ' if we never see them again:-[DOT]

Before we adjourn I wish, to notice that at some future meeting of this committee I intend to move a resolution that a report he made to the House recommending that in each of the purchasing departments an official be appointed whose duty it will be to certify as to the justness of accounts from the standpoint of prices before payment. I think the government of Canada should he in the same position as an ordinary individual; if they are buying small articles they are justified in going to a retailer and buying them. But we have had from the evidence that D. K. McLaren & Company are selling belting in one case at a discount of 50 per cent. It is not in evidence but it is in the Auditor General's Report that the same firm are selling belting at jobbers's discount. Now, we have also evidence that the Public Works Department have paid much greater prices than D. K. McLaren charged, less 50 per cent. That is, we have three sets of prices paid by the government for leather belting.
That motion has not been moved. I do not know that the government is to be accused, is to be found guilty upon isolated instances where agents of "theirs purchase articles such as leather belting at three or four times the price for which it can be purchased in the open market, but I do say that the government is responsible if, after a condition of affairs such as this is brought to their attention, they do not remedy it. In this case it was shown that in a purchase from Lymburner, Limited, of $800, there was a rake-off of $500 and I used the word ' rake-off,' advisedly. Yet on looking in the Auditor General's Report this year I have already found items showing purchases on the part of this government from the same firm of Lymburner, Limited, involving amounts of $4,137.40. There may be others but these I have found. I do not propose to labour this matter in detail, the facts are very simple. If the Public Accounts Committee is to be of any service to the people of this country, then

its proceedings must be free and untrammelled and when it is disclosed before that committee that a state of affairs exists such as was ashown in the case of Lymburner, Limited, the government should take notice of the facts to such an extent that the same evil would never occur again in the same quarter.

Mr. Speaker, I am surprised that the Prime Minister should object to this motion. I have known for some time that it is absolutely necessary for the Committee on Public Accounts in investigating the accounts of any one year to have access to the accounts of the preceding year. I have had that experience and have been prevented by members of the Public Accounts Committee, supporters of the government, from going back beyond the year the accounts of which we were examining. When these gentlemen were objecting in that way I supposed they were acting alone. I could not believe that the Prime Minister himself was supporting them, but when he objects to-day to our taking the last year's report, I feel that he must have advised those gentlemen at that time not to allow us to go back. In the present year I myself have had experience of cases in which it is absolutely necessary that we should have last year's Auditor General's Report. I know one item in the Marine and Fisheries Department which I wished to examine, but I was told that some of these payments were made previous to this year and of course we could not go into that item. In another case in the Interior Department an item I believe was delayed and placed in this year's account so that we could not examine the original item. I shall give the instance so that the Prime Minister may investigate;. The Interior Department paid a certain gentleman for work in that department in 1888-9. They also paid him a salary, in fact double salary, for doing other work in that same department. They held back the extra amount until after March, 1909, and then paid it to him. We cannot investigate the whole circumstances of the case because we cannot use the Auditor General's Report of last year. The Prime Minister a few years ago when we alleged that in several departments robbery, looting and thievery was taking place, said he was very much astonished that such representations should be made, but after the very first investigation into the ' Arctic ' he had to come down and acknowledge that there was some truth in the charges. When I asserted that there was robbery, looting and thievery in the Marine and Fisheries Department, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries was very indignant, but when we got part of an investigation-and only part of it-we showed that every statement we made was true. The same thing applied to the Public Works
Department, no doubt there was looting, robbery and thievery there by the middleman and yet the Minister of Public Works now asks us to name one middleman. Does he want one name?
Yes.
What about John Moore of St. John, N.B.?
He is not a middleman.
He knew nothing of dredging.
I never heard of his being a middleman.

He never knew anything about dredging, and did not the Minister of Public Works give him a contract last year at 90 cents a yard' for dredging when his engineer certified that 20 cents or 30 cents was a sufficient price?
After public tender.
The Minister of Public Works knows, if he states what he knows is true, that that contract was given to John D. Moore before any tender was publicly asked for.
Not at all.
I challenge the Minister of Public Works to deny that statement, that he told his department to give the contract to John D. Moore.

My hon. friend is entirely wrong. Public tenders were called for that work of dredging at a very exposed place at the mouth of the Gaspereau river, in New Brunswick. The Maritime Dredging Company had a dredge coining from the St. Lawrence river. I knew that that was a place where we could expect very few people to be willing to dredge. I sent word through the engineering department to the Maritime Company that if they stopped their dredge there and dredged for a short time until the tenders were due, we would pay them in the meantime, while they were dredging, the price of the lowest tender, if they were not the lowest tenderers, they would go down to the Bay of Fundy and the lowest tenderers would get the contract. That is exactly what took place.
I know the cir-. cumstances of that case.
I know them too.
The Maritime Dredging Company had purchased a dredge at Montreal, the old Gilbert dredge, at once the minister told John D. Moore, who is practically the Maritime Dredging Company-

I tell my hon. friend he is entirely mistaken as to that. The pur-

chase of that dredge, I have reason to know, had nothing whatever to do with dredging at the mouth of the Gaspereau river. It was being brought down to the Bay of Fundy for other dredging work entirely.

Mr. J. D. Moore was not in the dredging business before the Gaspereau contract. He purchased his first dredge at that time, and that contract was the first work he did. Immediately after that, the St. John ' Telegraph ' was purchased. There is no doubt in my mind that the difference between 30 cents a yard and 90 cents a yard was given to buy the St. John ' Telegraph'-every person knows what that is, what it was given for. Then, what about McAvity? Was not he a middleman? He get five to ten cents a yard from Mayes, and is not he to-day one of the largest middlemen in the Public Works Department?
That is something that took place before I became minister, and I know nothing about it.
But the minister knows it was proven

The minister knows it was not proven.
Mr. REID (Grenville)-that Mr. McAvity got five to ten cents a yard from the Mayes dredging contract. That was proven.
It was not proven.

I desire to say only a few words in answer to some observations of the Prime Minister (Sir* Wilfrid Laurier), which were intended to. show the inadvisability of referring the accounts of any previous year to the Public Accounts Committee. In the first place, I do not agree with the Prime Minister that it has been the invariable practice not to refer such accounts to the committee. As a matter of fact, we have the precedent of three years ago, when the accounts of two years were referred to the committee; and I am not aware that this course proved greatly detrimental to the public interest or that it occasioned any inconvenience. I am not going into the many matters that have been dealt with in this debate, but I would point out to the Prime Minister some reasons why we should follow now the course that was followed three years ago. In the first place, there was a very considerable delay last year, as I am informed, before the Public Accounts Committee took up the work of investigating the public accounts and Auditor General's Report. In the next place, after that investigation had been commenced, the work of the committee was put over more than once at the instance of the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) and the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell), as I am informed.
I think the hon. gentleman is misinformed.

1 do not pretend to have any personal knowledge of the matter, but I have made some inquiries as to why this proposal has been made, and this is the information that I have received. I am sure that it is the case so far as the hon. member for Carleton is concerned-that he had to be absent and the work of the committee was delayed during his absence. Another consideration is that the Public Accounts Committee last year met usually, I believe, only twice a week. The right hon. Prime Minister will realize that this allows very few meetings having regard to the enormous amount of work that the committee has to do, particularly in the light of what has been exposed here this afternoon as to the*oper-ations of the middleman in the various departments of this government. One would naturally think that the case which was put forward by my hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes)-a most glaring and astounding case, in which $850 or thereabouts was paid for goods that could have been bought for less than $300-I should have thought that that one instance of robbery of the public treasury would appeal to the right hon. gentleman to give the fullest possible opportunity for exposing every transaction of that kind. Another consideration is that the time of the Public Accounts Committee last session was given almost wholly to the affairs of the Public Works Department, and they did not get half through with the matters that should have been investigated in that department alone. Another consideration-and I state these only briefly, and do not wish to dwell upon them-is that, on account of the indisposition of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) last session, his department, as I understand it, was not touched at all by the committee-there was no investigation and no opportunity for investigation. Then, because the time of the committee was so much taken up with the Department of Public Works, the affairs of the Printing Bureau were hardly touched at all ; and, surely my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), in the light of the revelations that have been made before the session, and at the beginning of the session in the report of the Secretary of State, will hardly deny that there ought to be some investigation into the affairs of the Printing Bureau in recent years. There is the further consideration offered by my hon. friend from Grenville (Mr. Reid), that in many cases which are proper for investigation by the Public Accounts Committee, the items to be found in this year's accounts run into matters which appear in the accounts of previous years ; and I understand from members who have spoken here to-day that the accounts of previous years are not, in such cases,
allowed to be taken up without the special order of the House. My hon. friend from South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) has stated to the House that, in former years that was not the rule, but it does appear to be the rule now. This affords another very cogent reason why the accounts of last year at least should be referred to this committee. In view of these considerations, and of the fact that no detriment to the public interest can be imagined or surmised as arising from the reference of such account to the committee, the Prime Minister might very well conclude that the accounts of the previous year, as well as those of the year just closed, should be referred. I should expect him to go further and say that, on the demand of any member of the Public Accounts Committee, the accounts of any previous year, so far as they refer to any matter which he desires to investigate, ought to be referred to the committee without a moment's hesitation. As far as my right hon. friend's motion is concerned, it is of no value at all, it only tells this Public Accounts Committee to do what it may do at the present time without any such amendment. Further than that, it seems to be restrictive even of that which, as the hon. member for Lanark has explained, used to be the rule of the Public Accounts Committee in years gone by. So, inste.ad of bein# any advantage in the way of furthering investigations, it is really restrictive, because it seems to recognize the rule that the Public Accounts Committee must come back to this House before it can even touch items of by-gone years closely connected with items under investigation by that committee.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I was impressed by the argument of the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes) to the effect that Mr. Lymburner was practically accused of having charged an extra price, and that, though this was proved before the committee, still the same firm has been furnishing goods to the government. That was certainly a charge which inn pressed me. But my hon. friend knows as well as I do that if the amendment of the hon. member for Simcoe is defeated the committee will still be able to investigate the circumstances referred to by the hon. member for Cumberland. Three years ago there was a special reason why the whole accounts of the previous year were referred to a special committee, because I had to go away, and the session was shortened, and it was understood that the accounts of that year would be investigated in the ordinary course, and they were investigated in the following session. But I always understood the practice to be that which was stated by the hon. member for Lanark, that the Committee of Public Accounts is bound

to go back as far as necessary, and if that is the -case, then there is no necessity for the motion of the member for Simcoe.

It is quite true that the arrangement of three years ago was carried out under an agreement. But the reasons for that agreement were of exactly the same character as those I have urged this afternoon. On that occasion there was not time for a full investigation, because the session was cut short on account of the departure of the Prime Minister for the conference. Last year the Department of Marine and Fisheries was not touched, because the minister was indisposed, and no attempt was made to touch it. The Printing Bureau was not touched for the reason that our time was all taken up with the Department of the Minister of Public Works, and so all through. So it seems to me there is practically the same reason for referring the accounts of last year to the committee as the reason which prevailed three years ago.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, these were special cases, and if the motion of my hon. friend is for a special case also, it can be made before the Public Accounts Committee. It is said that the Department of Marine and Fisheries was not investigated on account of the absence of the minister. That is a very good reason why they were not investigated. But that is not at all the argument which is now made for departing from our practice and referring all the accounts of the previous year to the Public Accounts Committee.

I would like to refer to a remark of the hon. member for Grenville (Mr. Reid) regarding dredging in Westmorland county. speechtext: (Jacques Cartier), I call the attention of the government to the following announcement which appeared in the government organ, the ' Free Press ' of yesterday.

maintopic: TO BUILD NAVY SHIPS IN CANADA.

speechtext: The government will in the course of a few days ask for tenders for the construction of four cruisers of the Bristol type and for six destroyers of the improved River type, the plans and specifications having arrived from

the Admiralty and been adapted to Canadian conditions.
No firms outside of the British Empire will be allowed to tender.
It is expected that the competition will lay between a Canadian syndicate, Vickers, Sons and Maxim, and Harland and Wolff of Belfast.
The vessels will have to be built in Canada, and are expected to be ready for commission by 1914.
This item, which is one of considerable interest is sufficient to whet the curiosity of the House and of the public, and I think we are entitled to ask the government to let us know if really it is cruisers of the type mentioned in this newspaper, which are being built, and what is their tonnage. The tonnage of the projected cruisers was 4,800 tons. What is the tonnage of the present ships, their length, their width, the speed required, when the construction is to begin, when delivery is to be made, where they are to be constructed? I believe that the practice in England is that when the plans are determined on and the keel is about to be laid, the plans are open to the inspection of the public and published in the naval technical newspapers and the 'Naval Annual' long before the ships are launched. At any rate, I think we are entitled to some enlightenment with reference to this newspaper item. I would ask the Minister of Marine if he will not give us a little more information than has been given to the newspaper.

House went to committee to consider the following proposed resolution
Resolved, that it is expedient, in connection with the establishment of the International Joint Commission under the Waterways Treaty of January II, 1909, to provide, (a) that the Governor in Council be authorized to appropriate annually, out of the consolidated revenue fund, a sum not exceeding seventy-five thousand dollars towards the payment of the salaries of the commissioners to be appointed bv His Majesty on the recommendation of the Governor in Council, as well as the salaries of the secretary and other officers and employees, and also all other expenses which may be incurred by such commissioners, with the approval of the Minister of Public Works, together with one-half share of all reasonable and necessary joint expenses of the said commission, incurred by it and under the terms of Mr. MONK.
the said treaty, required to be paid in equal moieties by the high contracting parties, (b) That the commissioners may from time to time employ such clerical and other assistance as is deemed advisable, their compensation and expenses to be fixed at such amounts as may be determined by the commissioners and approved by the Minister of Public Works, and may expend an amount to be fixed by the Minister of Public Works, not in excess of three thousand dollars per annum, for office accommodation, equipment and supplies.

As the government is asking from parliament a considerable sum for the purpose of paying the salaries of the Canadian members of the International Joint Commission, which it is proposed to appoint under the terms of the Waterways Treaty of January, 1909, it might be well that I should call the attention of hon. gentlemen to the provisions of the treaty under which they are to act, in order that the committee may have a better understanding of the very important duties and the very heavy responsibilities which will devolve upon this International Joint Commission. I do not know that I can do this better than by referring to the different provisions of the treaty. Hon. gentlemen are no doubt aware that the treaty was signed at Washington on the 11th of January, 1909. The United States Congress has already made provision for the salaries of the commissioners to be appointed on behalf of the United States, and also for their expenses, and the amount which has been provided for at the last session of Congress is a sum not exceeding $75,000, the same amount for which we are now asking. It will be observed that the resolution fixes the maximum salaries of the commissioners, also the maximum salary of the secretary who is to be appointed by the Canadian section of the commission, also the amount for office accommodation, equipment and supplies. Of course, there will necessarily be considerable other expenses, such as the salaries of engineers, and the payments for clerical work, which it is impossible to fix definitely at the present time; but all these expenses must be certified to by the commissioners and approved by the Minister of Public Works before payment.

Is the $75,000 provided by the United States Congress supposed to pay all the expenses of this commission for_ a year, or only the salaries of the commissioners and perhaps those of their engineers and secretaries?
All the expenses.
That is not the case in the resolution you are about to propose.

Yes, because it is provided that the amount shall not exceed $75,000, and out of that amount the salaries of the commissioners and the secretary, the

cost of office accommodation, equipment and supplies, and all other expenses are to be met.
How many Canadian commissioners are there?	_

The treaty provides for three to be appointed by His Majesty and three to be appointed on the part of the United States. I think the preamble to the treaty very well sets forth the objects sought to be accomplished by the convention, which was entered into. It is as follows:-
His Majesty tlie King of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland and of the British Dominions beyond the seas, Emperor of India, and the United States of America, being, equally desirous to prevent disputes regarding the use of boundary waters and to settle all questions which ane now pending between the United States and the Dominion of Canada involving the rights, obligations or interests of either in relation to the other or to the inhabitants of the other, along their common frontier, and to make provision for the adjustment and settlement of all such questions as may hereafter arise, have resolved to eonclude a treaty in furtherance of these ends.
It will be seen by an examination of the treaty that these objects are all very carefully kept in view by the different provisions of the convention. There is first the settlement of all questions relating to boundary waters. Then provision is made for the settlement of all questions which are likely to arise involving the rights, obligations and interests of either in relation to the other along their common frontier; and the treaty even goes further than that, and provides that by mutual consent all questions of any kind that may arise between the two countries may be submitted to this International Commission. So that hon. gentlemen will see at once, even without my reading the different articles of the treaty, how very important are the duties which these commissioners will be called upon to perform. The first article provides :-
The high contracting parties agree that the navigation of all navigable boundary waters shall forever continue free and open for the purposes of commerce to the inhabitants and to the ships, vessels, and boats of both countries equally, subject, however, to any laws and regulations of either country, within its own territory, not inconsistent with such privilege of free navigation and applying equally and without discrimination to the inhabitants, ships, vessels, and boats of both countries.
It is further agreed that so long as this treaty shall remain in force, this same right of navigation shall extend to the waters of Lake Michigan and to all canals connecting boundary waters, and now existing or which may hereafter be constructed on either side of the line. Either of the high contracting parties may adopt rules and regulations gov-28 i
erning the use of such canals within its own territory and may charge tolls for the use [DOT] thereof, but all such rules and regulations and all tolls charged shall apply alike to the subjects or citizens of the high contracting parties, and the ships, vessels, and boats of both of the high contracting parties, and they shall be placed on terms of equality in the use thereof.
Then it provides that:
Each of the high contracting parties reserves to itself the exclusive jurisdiction and control over the use and diversion, whether temporary or permanent, of all waters on its own side of the line which in their natural channels would flow across the boundary or into boundary waters.
I may say that that is simply an affirmance of what has always been contended by the United States to be international law, and of what I do not think has been disputed by the jurists of this country, that is to say that so far as the waters which are wholly situate within the country are concerned, that country may make a diversion of these waters and prevent them from flowing into the boundary waters.

Did the United States take that stand in regard to rivers arising in Mexico and flowing into the southern part of the United States, or do they confine it to the rivers that originate in the United States and flow into Canada?

The United States have contended that it is a principle of international law that any country has the right to divert waters in its own country subject always, I may say, to the question of navigation. I do not think that they have contended that they would have a right to so divert the waters as to seriously or materially interfere with navigation; but in the matter of waters which might be required for purposes of irrigation, a very important case came up between the United States and Mexico, in reference to the waters of the Rio Grande. These waters were diverted and upon complaint being made by the Mexican government the matter was taken up by the Attorney General of the United States, and after a lengthy investigation the United States took the position that what had been done was perfectly legal and that the Mexican government had no right to complain. This is very important by reason of a situation which exists in western Canada, a situation which is of very great interest to the people of Saskatchewan and Alberta as well as to the people of Montana upon the United States side of the line. This being the view which is taken by the United States and which, so far as I am aware, is not disputed on the part of this country, it is very important to bear in mind that the clause to which I am now inviting the attention of the committee goes on to provide:

Any interference with or diversion from their natural channel of such waters on either side of the boundary, resulting in any injury on the other side of the boundary, shall give rise to the same rights and entitle the injured parties to the same legal remedies as if such injury took place in the country where such diversion or interference occuts; hut this provision shall not apply to cases already existing or to cases expressly covered by special agreement between the parties hereto.
Therefore, hon. gentlemen will see that as to all future cases the citizens of either country are placed in exactly the same position as a riparian proprietor lower down the stream would be nlaced in regard to any diversion of water by a private riparian owner further up the stream by which his rights would be interfered with. In other words, both nations, by the latter clause of this article, making provision for the reeog nition and payment by the country whose subject caused the injury, recognize that there would be the same obligation to make payment for that injury as if it was a question between citizens of the same country.

I do not quite understand how that works out. Stripped of unnecessary words the clause would read: It is agreed that any diversion from their natural channel of such waters shall entitle the injured parties to the same legal redress as if such injury took place in the country where such [DOT] diversion occurred. That is the way it would read if you left out immaterial words. What does that exactly mean? For example, suppose diversion takes place in the United States of waters in which the people of Alberta are interested. What are you going to do about that?

It is provided that the people of Alberta shall have the same right to proceed in the courts of the United States as they would have to proceed in the courts of Alberta if the diversion had taken place in Alberta, that is to say the United States will have a perfect right to divert the water yet that diversion must be subject to the right of the person lowbr down the stream, whether in the United States or in Canada, to the same right of action against the upper riparian proprietor as if both people were subjects of the same country.

I understand the suggestion. A citizen of Alberta will go into the United States courts, I presume in Montana and bring an action; but suppose the diversion has been authorized by a statute of the United States.

Then I take it it would be the duty of both countries, the United States government in this case, the duty of the Canadian government if the diver-Mr. PUGSLEY.
sion were authorized by our government to make provision for the payment of any damages. That would be the obligation of each party under the terms of this treaty.

If the minister's statement could be a'dded as a rider to the treaty it would make it very plain, but there is nothing in the treaty to that effect. On the contrary there is a direct statement that the United States reserves absolute jurisdiction and control over that very thing, and therefore can pass such a statute as I have alluded to without apparently infringing the terms of this treaty, rather in accordance with its very terms. Then the citizen would not have in the United States the same rights as he would have if the diversion had taken place in Alberta. Therefore I do not think that you could work out the provisions of the treaty in the way the minister suggests.

This article does not profess to give to either country the right to divert water; it simply reserves to each country the right already existing and the right which would be exercised without the riparian owner lower down the stream having any possible remedy. This article provides that if the diversion is done by an individual there shall be the same right for a citizen of this country to go to Montana and bring an action as -a citizen of Montana would have if the diversion took place in Montana and vice versa.

I am not so sure as the minister is that it is a recognized principle of international law that one country or its citizens under its laws can divert a stream that runs into an adjoining country. I have always had it in mind, although I have not looked carefully into the question, that the general rule of international law was quite the reverse of that.

We have had a very striking example of that right being claimed on the part of the United States and being acquiesced in by the various governments of this country for 40 or 50 years in the case of the Allegash river in the state of Maine. The Allegash river naturally flowed into the St. John river. As much as forty or fifty years ago, the legislature of the state of Maine authorized a company to divert the waters of the Allegash into the Penobscot at a place called Chamberlain lake, which is at the summit. By putting a dam at the foot of Chamberlain lake, the waters of the Allegash were thrown back into the Penobscot. There was a canal dug also. Some controversy took place and some international correspondence passed, but the government which was in power at the time when the diversion took place did not appear to think-and I presume it was so advised-that there could be any

claim made against the United States, but that the Americans had the right to do what was done. In that case-and it makes the case of the Allegash even stronger than an ordinary case would be,-it might be contended that the diversion of the waters of the Allegash interferred to some extent with the navigation of the St. John river. It certainly interfered with the floatability of the river for the purpose of driving logs.
Mr.	CROCKET.	Does not	the treaty
make an end to the controversy as to the Allegash ?
Mr.	PUGSLEY.	Except as	to navigation.

And ends it in favour of the United States?
Mr.	PUGSLEY.	Except as	to navigation.	I take it that	where rights have not
been asserted, or have been asserted only at rare intervals and not successfully, and where the diversion took place some fifty years ago and has existed for fifty years, it would be too late to expect that any remedy would be applied. But it has always been contended that any rights which the people of New Brunswick had to have the waters of Chamberlain lake turned back into the St. John river depended upon the question of navigation. It was contended that the diversion of the waters interfered with the floatability of the St. John river for the purpose of driving logs, and that I think, in this country, would be taken as affecting navigation. However, whatever these rights are they are expressly reserved by the treaty.

The point I referred to, I would like to thresh out a little, if the minister will bear with me, is this: If the diversion in Montana takes place under the authority of a statute, citizens of Alberta, coming into the courts of Montana would have no right of action. The minister suggests that the two governments would get together in some way and provide damages or compensation. But I do not find that in the treaty or anything like it.

One would not expect to find it in the treaty, I think. My hon. friend is aware that if the legislature of the province of Alberta chose to authorize an injury to be done by one riparian proprietor to another and did not provide for compensation there would be no right to compensation. But it is not supposed that any legislature, where the right is expressly recognized by law, would take away that right without providing compensation. The important provision in this article is that it gives to the people of both countries the right of action which they have not heretofore enjoyed, and it also recognizes the principle that they shall have the same
right to compensation or damages, as if they were both residing in the state or province in which the injury was committed. That, I think, is a very important principle to have recognized.
The principle may be a very good one, but it strikes me that the right of action may prove entirely vain and illusory.

While dealing with that feature, as I am not a lawyer, there are one or two points I would like explained. The state of Montana controls its waters, but the province of Alberta does not control its waters. The federal government in Canada has the right to deal with the waters in Alberta, while the federal government at Washington, as I understand it, has no such right. Now, if the legislature of Montana gave certain rights to parties to withdraw water-to put water to beneficial use-in Montana, and some interest on the Canadian side should be injured, I understand the minister to say that, on failure to reach a settlement the-two governments would step in. This treaty is with the federal government at Washington, which, as I understand it, has nothing to do with the waters in question.

I am satisfied that it is recognized as law in the United States that, as the treaty-making power rests with the government of the United States, a treaty, when it comes into force, binds all the states of the Union, and so, this treaty will govern the rights of the different states in respect of any of the waters dealt with by the treaty.

I was not aware that there was any provision in the constitution of the United States to that effect. There is a provision in the British North America Act that the parliament of Canada shall have the right to enact any legislation that may be necessary to carry out the terms of a treaty. I have no very exhaustive knowledge of the constitution of the United States, but I am not aware that it contains any similar provision. I speak rather from recollection of facts which are common knowledge, that there have been difficulties in carrying out treaties with the United States-the federal government has said, over and over again, that it has no control over the states in respect of certain matters.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend (Mr. R. L. Borden), is right ; there is no such provision in the American constitution. And I may go further and say that my hon. friend knows, and everybody knows, that, in the days of the extreme State's Rights party in the United States, it was also contended that the treaty-making power did not apply

against the rights of the states. But I understand-though I have not looked into the case recently-that the doctrine is now accepted in the United States that the treaty-making power dominates the state rights and makes the law of the land. I have not studied the question, but that 1 understand from American jurists.
It is very important that we should know something definite about that in view of the points raised by my hon. friend from Medicine Hat (Mr. Magrath).

The same question has come up in regard to fishing in the lakes. I am not in a position to-night -to tell my hon. friend where the principle is authoritatively stated, but I know that it is recognized by the law officers of the government of the United States. They have dealt with the fisheries entirely upon that principle. By the treaty they have dealt with the fisheries of the states bordering on the Great Lakes. The legal authorities assert, without apparent question as to the authority of the statement, that, under the treaty the state rights must give way so far as the treaty is concerned.
I do not know whether the hon. minister objects to being interrupted now, or whether he would rather have the discussion take place afterwards-

I will take occasion to look into the question raised by the hon. member (Mr. Magrath). This resolution is to be followed by a Bill, of course, and I will give every opportunity for the discussion of this matter on the second reading or in committee.

I might remind the minister and the leader of the opposition of a case in point which has probably escaped their attention, where treaty powers have conflicted with state rights in the United States. I refer to the case of the California schools where trouble arose about two years ago on account of the state legislature passing a law preventing Japanese children from attending the public schools. This law was clearly in contravention of the Japanese treaty with the United States, and the state government had to abandon their contention on the ground that the treaty gave a special privilege to the Japanese children. That is a case in point, showing that in the United States a treaty was considered superior to state rights.
One more question. I understand the minister's opinion is that under that article vested rights against a stream on one side of the boundary must be honoured on the other side.

Exactly, that is the spirit of the treaty, that is what it is intend-
Sir WILFRID LAUR1ER.
ed to provide, and it is giving an absolutely new right to subjects of the two countries.

This question of conflicting jurisdiction is liable to come up frequently. For instance, it is well established in the United States that the federal government has the right to make treaties in all matters where citizenship or the rights of citizens are concerned; but in matters relating to private property the state has always raised objections to federal action. I do not think that there is any decision that will clear the matter up to the satisfaction of this House. The controversy has arisen in several cases. There was a case at the Sault where property was held for a millwright, and some compromise was arrived at, leaving the question not yet definitely settled. We have this matter coming up again and again. This country goes into the business of making a treaty with the United States, goes into it with clean hands and with federal rights unchallenged. On the other side there is just that danger that the old question of state rights may be involved and may crop up. It is very doubtful whether, in a matter of international law, private property for instance could be expropriated for treaty purposes. That is virtually what is here proposed. Now there is another point with reference to this. I would like to know from the minister if the present commission has established a boundary line in Lake Ontario and Lake Erie. The reason I ask is this: I think if that boundary line has >een established it is desirable that a copy of the map of that part of it in Niagara river should be laid on the table of this House. I understand from information I obtained in the United States that there was a question with reference to the waterpower of Niagara Falls. The original boundary was clearly defined by the commissioners established undeff the treaty and could easily be found to-day. In the division of the territory then the Horse shoe Falls were given entirely to Canada. We have there a large amount of power now belonging to the province of Ontario. The United States set up a claim for one-half of the water-power, virtually, of the Niagara river. Now I understand that this commission which is now establishing these waterways and this boundary- there are two commissions, I do not know whether it is this one or the boundary commission-one of them has gone to work and is laying down a new line and a neiv boundary depriving the province of Ontario of its rights to the whole of the Horseshoe Falls. If that is the case I think the minister should so state in the House now, and take an early opportunity to lay the whole matter before the House, so that we may know whether that boundary is going to be altered. This is a very important matter.

It is a grave commentary on the contention of this government in the matter of treaties, since they have always been claiming that Great Britain has surrendered territory belonging to Canada in the past, and it would be a singular thing if this government now make a surrender of territory which has been clearly established to be ours by treaty, by definite survey and by landmarks.

That is the very point I mention. This commission may do all the damage possible, and the moment you have appointed this new commission there is nobody to blame for it. Now, I think that before the debate on the Bill takes place, the hon. gentleman should lay on the table of this House a plan of the surveys of the Niagara river, and the boundary established there as it now exists at this date.
I will be glad to do that.

It is all right to establish a boundary line along the centre of the lakes, because in the old days it was very hard to establish. But there is no question as to where the boundary was laid down in the Niagara river by the former commissioners, and there is no necessity for changing that now, which I understand is being done.

I was going to call attention to the fact that the remaining clause of this article provides expressly :
Each of the hivh contracting parties reserves to iteelf or to the several state governments on the one side and the Dominion or provincial governments on the other as the case may be, subject to any treaty provisions now existing with respect thereto, the exclusive jurisdiction and control over the use and diversion, whether temporary or permanent,_ of all waters on its own side of the line which in their natural channels would flow across the boundary or into boundary waters.
The effect of that is to provide, that so far as ordinary streams are concerned, the high contracting parties reserve jurisdiction over the use and diversion of the waters of those streams, subject always to the right of compensation, and then each country reserves to itself the right to protest just the same as it could do before this treaty was agreed to, against any diversion which would interfere with navigation.

I would mention the case of a province which owns or controls its own waters. Take for instance the province of Ontario, which has the ownership of all its own waters, subject to the superior law of the federal authorities over navigation. Under article 2 of this treaty not only all waters are governed by this treaty, but all waters which flow across the boundary, or waters which flow into boundary waters, are subject to this provision. ' Boundary waters ' is a very large term. It would include, as I apprehend, the waters adjacent to the Great Lakes, such as Georgian bay ajid the rivers flowing into Georgian bay. These waters always have been and are still notoriously provincial waters. They are being dealt with by this treaty. The rights of riparian holders are being dealt with and they are being very seriously affected. If they interfered with the flow of these waters they would be liable in damages to a lumberman or citizen of the state of Michigan, New York, or any other state. Has the government taken any steps with regard to consulting the different provinces or is it acting in co-operation with the provinces, such as the province of Ontario or any other province, which owns adjacent waters, before disposing of these waters or of the riparian rights in them?

The rights of the provinces are in no way affected. The province of Ontario to-day may divert the waters of any streams flowing into the Great Lakes within that province. All that this treaty provides for is that if any American citizen suffers damage by reason of the diversion he will have the right to compensation, and if, on the other hand, one of the United States bordering on the Great Lakes, diverts waters that are tributary to the Great Lakes and a resident of Ontario suffers damage, he shall be entitled

to claim compensation. In so far as the' power of the different provinces and states is concerned, it is in no way interfered with. All that this treaty does is to provide an equitable mode for the people of each country to obtain compensation from the people of the other country in case their rights are in any way affected. I am sure the committee will realize that there are very few cases-perhaps there never would be a case-where this question would arise except in the case of waters which are used for the purpose of irrigation. The question might arise between the inhabitants of Montana, Alberta and Saskatchewan, because a person or company in Montana might divert certain waters which flow to the northward and use these waters for the purposes of irrigation. The result might be to deprive a Canadian living lower down the stream upon the Canadian side of the boundary of water which would be very necessary for the purpose of irrigation. Before this treaty that could be done and he could not say a word, but under this treaty he can complain through this government, I take it, to the authorities of the United States, and it would be their duty, in carrying out the spirit of this treaty, to see that compensation is provided for the injury, and, vice versa, the same obligation that is imposed upon the people of the United States is also imposed upon the people of Canada.
Just a word as to the question of the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Magrath) as to the right of the United States government to make a treaty which will bind the states which, as my hon. friend says, are the owners of these waters.
I find by article 6 of the Constitution of the United States that this point is clearly settled. That article provides:-
That this constitution and the laws of the United States which shall be made in pursuance thereof and all treaties made or which shall he made under the authority of the United States 6liall be the supreme law of the land and the judges in every state shall he bound thereby, anything in the constitution or laws of any state to the contrary notwithstanding.
That seems to make it absolutely clear that the treaty-making power of the government of the United States extends to, the waters of the various states and also to the fisheries of the various states.

Following that up, will the minister cite or quote what power this government has on the other hand to deal with provincial waters such as belong to tthei provinces in whom these waters are vested-Ontario as an example?

This is a treaty made between His Majesty the King of Great Mr. PUGSLEY.
Britain and Ireland and the dominions beyond the seas, and this treaty is the supreme law of the empire as far as Canada is concerned, just the same, as far as the United States is concerned, it is the supreme law of the United States, and every state is bound by it.
Has it become effective without ratification by parliament?
Yes.
That is not the case in the United States, where every treaty must receive the ratification of the Senate.
There the Senate is the treaty-making power, just as with us the King is the treaty-making power.

It is an extraordinary thing that this government, after the protest that was made in this House last session, would permit of the imposition of a special rider in this treaty discriminating against and making special provision with reference to private rights in St. Mary's river. I do not understand it.
We will come to that later on.

If, as the Minister of Public Works- has stated, this treaty is to be supreme between the two nations, why did the government consent to a rider being attached to it, which recognizes riparian, territorial and other rights in the waters of the St. Mary's river? Why, with regard to _ all other rivers and waters with which this treaty presumes to deal, are these rights merged in the supreme right of the high compact when the rights with regard to St. Mary's river are singled out, and given separate treatment. It was pointed out to the right hon. Prime Minister, I think in as cogent a manner as it possibly could be done, having regard to the facts at our disposal, that there was a dangerous encroachment on Canadian territory in the St. Mary's river, and I would like to know why these dangers were made more dangerous by this rider and why that rider was consented to by the government, if the law is as it is stated to be by the Minister of Public Works?

I will come to that a little later on because that rider is at the last of the treaty. I am sure that my hon. friend (Mr. Boyce), will not think that I am discourteous to him, if I deal with that provision of the treaty later.

With regard to that article, the last paragraph indicates that waters used for navigation purposes shall not be disturbed. I understand that is the substance of the last paragraph of the treaty, and if that is so, there is this point that I would like to bring to the attention of

the hon. gentleman. Streams run into each other, or rather they are made up of smaller streams. Take the Missouri river. It is difficult to navigate properly in certain seasons. It is fed by a great number of these streams which cross from Alberta and Saskatchewan. By the diversion .of these streams in Canada you might interfere with the navigation of the Missouri river. Would it be possible for our friends to the south of us to say: You must not disturb these streams in Canada, because, while they are not navigable themselves, they go to feed a stream which is navigable or partially so?
My hon. friend, I think is aware that this question could only arise in respect to the Milk river, and its tributaries. Am I not right in that? [DOT]
No, 1 do not think so. We have two or three thousand miles of boundary and that feature might arise at various other points.
Not with regard to streams running into the Missouri?
No.
If my hon. friend is right then the Milk river is the only river, which flows into the Missouri from Canada?
I merely mentioned that as an instance to bring the point to the hon. gentleman's attention.

Of course, if we go to the little streams which are tributaries of the larger streams and which are again tributaries of the rivers which are not navigable, and which finally become tributaries of the navigable streams of the United States it would be difficult to say that even the use of the water in a small stream for domestic purposes does not remove a certain quantity, even though it might be infinitesimal, of water, and keep it away from the deep river which is navigable.
But, what the two governments have done has been to endeavour upon the broadest possible basis to try to provide a means for,settling these international and irritating questions, which are liable to arise from time to time. As my hon. friend will admit, so far as the Missouri is concerned, that is a river in regard to which I suppose one of the most important questions would be likely to arise; indeed, the only important question so far. as diversion for irrigation purposes is concerned, because happily we do not have to use water for purposes of irrigation in the east. The Milk river is the only river which flows from the Canadian side into the Missouri. The Milk river takes its rise in the state of Montana, and the Milk river and the St. Mary's river are the two principal rivers which are
essential for purposes of irrigation in that western country, and both of them have their source in the United States. Under the principles of international law I am inclined to think that there would be no question that the United States government, but for this treaty, would have the power to divert the waters of both these rivers before they flowed over the Canadian boundary and so deprive the people of Alberta and Saskatchewan of the use of these waters for purposes of irrigation. We know that in the west, water for irrigation purposes is almost priceless, and if the United States had exercised the right which they held they were entitled to exercise and were to divert these streams down towards the Missouri river and prevent them flowing into Canada they would have caused irreparable injury to the people of the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. We have by this treaty provided against the possibility of anything of that kind occurring. When I come to the article which especially deals with the St. Mary's and the Milk rivers I think hon. gentlemen will agree with me that in concluding this treaty the United States, powerful country that it is, has shown a spirit of justice, a spirit of exceeding fair play towards the people of Canada. I think every one will agree that the treaty is eminently fair and makes the most valuable provision for safeguarding the rights of the people of Canada, as well as Ube rights of the people of the United States with regard to these rivers.

I appreciate the hon. minister's oration about the justness of this treaty with the United States and the inestimable value of water in that western country, those subjects, and the extent to which he has protected the rights of Canada I shall have something to say when the Bill comes down. But, I have put a practical question to the minister. I mentioned the Missouri river. Now the minister appears to be expending money in the development of the Saskatchewan river for navigation purposes. Suppose we reverse the situation. There is the St. Mary's river flowing north into this country and supplementing the supply of the south Saskatchewan river. I have seen boats on that river some 25 years ago, and there was not any too much water to permit of navigation. Under this treaty the provision I have just referred to in the concluding paragraph of the article says that navigation interests shall not be interfered with. The point I raise is this-take the St. Mary's river, a very important stream upon which navigation is not possible, but is it not possible that bv diverting the St. Mary's river into the United .States and withdrawing its supply from the Saskatchewan river, you will put the Saskatchewan

river out of business so far as navigation is concerned. That is thu point I was referring to.

Of course the same question would arise so far as Canada is concerned with regard to the Milk river. Suppose you were to utilize the Milk river in the 100 miles over which it flows through Canadian territory and take its water for the purpose of irrigation, thus preventing it flowing down to the Missouri, the United States would have just as much ground for complaint as we could have in the case of the St. Mary's river. But I want to say, if my hon. friend (Mr. Magrath) will pardon me, that the high contracting parties have left by this treaty the rights to each country, so far as navigation is concerned, exactly where these rights were before the treaty. There is this provision:-
It is understood that neither of the high contracting parties intend by the foregoing provision to surrender any right which it may have to object to any interference with, or diversions of waters on the other side of the boundary, the effect of which would be productive of material injury to the navigation interests on its own side of the boundary.
The treaty leaves that question concerning the rights of the two countries exactly' where they were before; it does not interfere with these rights in the least degree.
I realize what the minister has said; I was really endeavouring to- get from the minister an interpretation of the language in the treaty.
I could hardly be expected to do that off-hand, because it is a very important question.
Am I to understand that a copy of these maps and the delimitation of the boundary of the Niagara river will be laid on the table when this Bill next comes before us?

Yes, so far as they are prepared. I do not know how far the preparation of the maps has proceeded, but I will make inquiry and give the hon. gentleman information. Some considerable time ago I was spoken to with regard to the survey which was being made, and 1 would suppose that there would be maps and reports sufficiently far advanced to be laid on the table. I will give my hon. friend an opportunity for further time for consideration if he so wishes, after I have given him information as to the maps.

I understand that the maps are being drawn on copper plates and that proofs of them have been taken from time to time, as they proceeded with the work. I understand that this commission has settled the boundary of Niagara Falls, and I would like to see where that boundary has been placed.
I will be glad to get these reports.

I would like to understand definitely from the minister whether the waters in the province of Ontario have been dealt with, as they are dealt with in article II. of the treaty, without the government of Ontario being in any way consulted.

My hon. friend is entirely wrong. The waters of Ontario have not been dealt with at all. If the treaty has done anything so far as the waters of Ontario are concerned, it has reserved to the people of Ontario the right to do as they pleased with their waters, subject only to the right of compensation.
Whatever the dealings have been in regard to these waters in the province of Ontario, under article II. of this treaty, they have been arrived at without that province being in any way consulted.
Will the hon. gentleman tell me of one stream in the province of Ontario which flows into a boundary water or which this treaty interferes with or affects in the slightest degree?

I certainly will. Although the hon. minister should, I think, have courteously answered my question, still I will answer his. The treaty deals with boundary waters or waters which flow into boundary waters. As a sample of waters which are boundary waters, and yet through which the boundary line does not pass, take the Georgian bay, the centre of which is hundreds of miles from where the international boundary runs through Lake Huron and Lake Michigan. These are treated as boundary waters, and the rivers and streams that flow into the Georgian bay and Lake Simcoe are also treated as boundary waters. These are provincial streams subject only to the greater right of the Dominion in regard to navigation. I ask the minister if, in dealing with these waters under article II. of this treaty, the provincial government of Ontario has in any way been consulted.

It is possible that the chairman of the International Deep Waterways Commission may have conferred with the Ontario government. I do not know as to that. I refer to Mr. Gibbons, who had a great deal to do with assisting the British ambassador in looking afteT the making of the treaty. I am not aware that there was any conference with the Ontario government; but the treaty cannot by any possibility give any ground for complaint on the part of the province of Ontario. The streams which flow into the Georgian bay are not touched by the treaty excepting so far as

navigation is concerned, and the treaty expressly reserves to the people of Canada and the people of the United States the right to protest against any interference with navigation.
Will the minister say that the provincial authorities of New Brunswick are not interested in the diversion of the waters of the Allegash river?

The people of New
Brunswick are very deeply interested. I do not know that the provincial authorities are more interested than the people are, and this government has been very careful to safeguard the interests of the people of New Brunswick.
I understood the minister to admit that this treaty had concluded that controversy in favour of the United States.
No, it has not concluded it at aill. It has done nothing about it in one way or the other.

The minister stated that that controversy was concluded by this treaty. That is a matter in which the provincial authorities are very much interested, and I would like to know if before the treaty was concluded they were consulted as to its terms.

I fear I did not make myself understood by my hon. friend. What I said was that the right to divert a stream which would injuriously affect navigation, is not given to either country, but the right to protest is reserved to each country. Each country had the same right to deal with such streams before the treaty that it has to-day. What the treaty does is to give to the inhabitants of either country the right to compensation from those who do injury in that connection. The people of New Brunswick never had that right before.

That is an entirely new right. But for this treaty the residents of the United States would not have that right-is that not correct? Remedies are given in favour of citizens of the United States in cases where the streams in Canada have been diverted or in any way interfered with. Before this treaty those persons would have no such right of action against citizens of this country. I ask, is it not so that under this treaty and only under it such rights of action would arise in favour of citizens of the United States?

My hon. friend is right in that-and also in favour of citizens of Canada. This right of compensation is a new right which is given to the citizens of either country. To that extent it might be said that it would be of interest to the people of a province where water could be
diverted by citizens of the United States to the injury of the people of that province, and vice versa. With regard to the Allegash river, I did not intend to say and I do not think I did say that this treaty has concluded the question with regard to that river.
Except in so far as navigation is concerned.

What I did say was that this treaty leaves the question of the Allegash just where it was before. If its diversion does not interfere with navigation. we had no right to make any claim against the United States before, and we have just as much right to-day to make a claim as we ever had. If its diversion interferes with navigation, we expressly reserve the right to protest, and that right is recognized by this treaty.

What does this clause in article II. mean:	'By this provision
shall not apply to cases already existing' ? I thought it was in connection with that clause that the minister made the statement that the Allegash controversy was concluded by the terms of the treaty.

No. What I meant to say and did say was that this treaty in no way deals with a diversion which took place before the treaty was negotiated. The only thing provided for is that there is no claim for damages which took place before the treaty came into force.

As I understand article II. of the treaty gives the right of action in certain cases to citizens on one side of the line against citizens on the other side; but immediately afterwards it says: 'This provision shall not apply to cases already existing.' Does that not include cases like the Allegash?

Quite so, but that refers to questions of damages. So far as the right to recover damages is concerned, this treaty relates wholly to future diversions; but so far as the right to make a claim against the nation for previous diversions is concerned, that right remains exactly as it was before the treaty was made. Nothing is added or taken away. The right to protest against interference with navigation remains as it was. It has not been sacrificed or altered in any shape or form.
At any rate, I understand that the provincial government of New Brunswick was not consulted at all in regard to the terms of the treaty?
Not at all.

It is very evident that this treaty does put forward a new principle-that under this treaty compensation is possible to the citizens of either country.

The minister admits that as rather an advantage in equity to the citizens of both countries. Has the minister or has the government made any careful estimate through its engineers as to the proportion of streams which flow southward from Canada into boundary waters or northward from the United States into boundary waters? If 75 per cent of these streams flow southward, it is obvious that the provision of this article will work very strongly to the advantage of the United States because their claims for compensation will be 75 per cent as against our 25 per cent. It would be interesting to get information along that line.

I have not made a careful calculation because it would be impossible to make one which would be of any value as the question would not depend on the number of streams there were, but on the number of diversions which would be likely to take place, and that would depend, of course, on the question of irrigation, and, as my hon. friend will see, upon many other questions which might arise.

I cannot see the strength of the point raised. Surely there is some reasonable ground for asking as to the total number of streams, a comparison of the flow, as it would work out in the end that the same percentage of diversion would be possible in one case as the other, and if 80 per cent were flowing south and 20 per cent north, the diversion would be the same, and we would be suffering great disadvantages as compared with the United States in regard to compensation.

Diversions are not likely to take place except for irrigation. There might be. some slight diversion in regard to the development of power, but the water so diverted is again turned into the streams, and the flow is not reduced. In the case of irrigation it is different because when water is taken from a stream and used for irrigation it flows over and sinks into the land and is lost to the stream. As far as the irrigation district is concerned, I would think, from my study of the different rivers, it is about equal.
