The high contracting parties have made special provision with regard to the Milk and St. Mary's rivers, to which I shall invite the attention of the committee a little later.
The next article provides for certain important duties which are to be performed by the representations of the two' countries. That article is as follows:
It is agreed that, in addition to the uses, obstructions, and diversions heretofore permitted or hereafter provided for by special pgreemienit between (the (parties hereto, no further or other usee or obstructions or diversions, whether temporary or permanent, of boundary waters on either side of the line, Mr. BURRELL.
affecting the natural level or flow of boundary waters on the other side of the line, shall be made except by authority of the United States or the Dominion of Canada within their respective jurisdictions and with the approval, as hereinafter provided, of a joint commission to be known as the International Joint Commission.
The foregoing provisions are not intended to limit or interfere with the existing rights of the government of the United States on the one side and the government of the Dominion of Canada on the other, to undertake and carry on governmental works in boundary waters for the deepening of channels, the construction of breakwaters, the improvement of harbours, and other governmental works for the benefit of commerce and navigation, provided that such work6 are wholly on its own side of the line and do not materially affect the level or flow of the boundary waters on the other, nor are such provisions intended to interfere with the ordinary use of such waters for domestic and sanitary purposes.
That imposes, as hon. gentlemen will see, a very great responsibility upon this commission. They are to investigate cases which may arise from time to time of proposed development, proposed diversion of water which might affect the navigation of the boundary waters and it is their duty to investigate each case; before any such diversion takes place it must be by authority of the United States or the Dominion of Canada within their respective jurisdictions and it must have the approval of this joint commission.

Will not this joint commission then take the place of the present commission that has been sitting for the last year or two with regard to the river St. John as a boundary river, and if so what will become of the work of the present commission? Has that commission made any report to the government or the Department of Public Works, and by what authority was that commission appointed. They have been working for some time and must have been working under some authority and with some end in view. While the minister is referring to this article he might give us an explanation of the position of that commission, whether it is a joint commission and what its future will be.

I have no doubt my hon. friend is aware that some few years ago a lumber company called the St. John Lumber Company, incorporated under the laws of the State of Maine, proceeded toward the construction of a saw-mill and also of booms, sheer dams, dams and sorting works upon the United States side of the St. John river. The lumbermen operating further down the St. John river, both in St. John and Fredericton, and I think also in other places, claimed that this was a violation of the Ashburton treaty, that under that treaty the waters

of the St. John river were to be kept open, free and unobstructed, to the commerce of both countries, and that by erecting these dams, piers, booms and sorting works, the floatability of that portion of the river was interfered with. Protests were made to the United States government and, without going fully into the details, finally an understanding was reached by which a commission was appointed, two members being appointed by the United States government and two by the Canadian government to consider the question of these obstructions. Provision was made for the salaries and expenses of the commissioners by this parliament and that provision has been renewed from time to time. Afterwards their duties were enlarged so as to authorize them, indeed they were instructed to consider the question of the possibility of storing the waters of the St. John and its tributaries so as to provide a more even flow of water, a greater flow during the dry season and so adding to the navigability and floatibility of the river, more especially for the purpose of lumber driving.
They have been engaged with engineers in taking the evidence of people who have had experience on the St. John river. They have had surveys made and have made an examination into the feasibility of constructing storage works and have devoted a good deal of time to the performance of the duties to which they were appointed. They have not submitted a report; but I had word a few days ago from the Canadian branch of the Commission stating that, if it was thought advisable, they would submit a preliminary report and asking my opinion. I wrote that I thought it would be well to have a preliminary report, that we might be informed of the work they have done up to the present time. I have no doubt that that report will soon be presented. As to whether their duties will cease on the appointment of this commission, I am not so sure; I should think that a matter for the consideration of the two governments. It might be-and I am at the moment inclined to think it would be-better that they should continue until they have completed the special work for which they have been appointed and have made a report. I do not imagine that it will take very much longer to complete the work. They have no authority to enter upon expenditure for storage or other works; they are an advisory body. We hope they will agree upon a recommendation to the two governments with regard not only to this question of the alleged obstruction of the St. John river by the works to which I have referred, but also on the question of erecting storage works to improve the navigability of the river.

Are they expected to decide whether the booms and other works
on the river which they were appointed to inquire into are obstructions and in contravention of the treaty?
It will be quite within their power to express an opinion to the respective governments upon the question whether these works are obstructions or not.
But they have no power to order them away?
No; they are simply to make a report for the information of the two governments.

Referring to the first clause of this article:-
It is agreed that, in addition to the uses, obstructions and diversions heretofore permitted or hereafter provided for-
And so on. Could it be held that these are obstructions that have been permitted, and so to be left there under this article, without leaving it open for the government of Canada to object?
This would not affect the rights of the respective parties under the Ashburton Treaty.
What is meant by the words I have just read?
That would mean, permitted by the two countries.
And would not apply to the case of the St. John river?

I do not think it would.
The next article provides:-
The high contracting parties agree that, except in cases provided for by special agreement between them, they will not permit the construction or maintenance on their lospective sides of the boundary of any remed' ial or protective works or any dams or other obstructions in waters flowing from boundary waters or in waters at a lower level than the boundary in rivers flowing across the boundary, the effect of which is to raise the natural level of waters on the other side of the boundary unless the construction or maintenance thereof is approved by the aforesaid International Joint Commission.
It is further agreed that the waters herein defined as boundary waters and waters flowing across the boundary shall not be polluted on either side to the injury of health or property on the other.
Here, the House will see, is another very important duty imposed on these commissioners. They are to inquire into any remedial works it is proposed to construct the effect of which would be to raise the level of the water upon the other side of the boundary than that on which they are constructed, and such works are not to be carried on without their consent. The

next provision is for the division of the water-power at Niagara.
In view of the special and onerous duties that this commission is to perform, I suppose the minister proposes to appoint able, skilled engineers having technical knowledge of the matters dealt with?

The question of the appointees to the Commission has not come before the government for consideration. But I would agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Macdonell), that the duties and responsibilities of this Joint Commission will be so great that only men eminently fitted for the discharge of these duties should be appointed; I am sure my hon. friend will have enough confidence in the government to believe that when the time comes to make the appointments, the government will be guided by this consideration.
Will the minister please state who are the present members of the board?

The Canadian members are: Mr. Gibbons, of London, Mr. Louis Coste, and Mr. Stewart, of Ottawa. The appointments are to be made by the imperial government, upon the recommendation, of course, of the governor in council.
I do not know whether the hon. minister wishes to discuss that feature of the matter now, or whether he would rather go through the treaty.

I think it would be better to go through the treaty. The next provision, as I have said, is for the division of the waters at Niagara Palls. I need not go into that further than to say that it is provided that the United States may authorize the diversion of the waters above the Falls for power purposes to the extent of not more daily than at the rate of 20,000 cubic feet per second, while the United Kingdom, the Dominion, or the province may authorize the diversion to an extent not exceeding in the aggregate daily 36,000 cubic feet per second.

The Joint International Waterways Commission made recommendations regarding the Chicago Drainage Cana! which have not appeared in the treaty. Is the minister at liberty to state why their recommendations in that respect were not embodied in the treaty?

I am not able to say. I am not familiar with the recommendations they made on that subject.
Article 6 is a very important article and one of special interest to the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan and to the state of Montana. It is as follows:-

The high contracting parties agree that the St. Mary and Milk rivers and their tributaries (in the state of Montana and the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan) are to be treated as one stream for the purposes of irrigation and power, and the waters thereof shall be apportioned equally between the countries, but in making such equal apportionment more than half may be taken from one river and less than half from the other l.y either country so as to afford a more beneficial use to each. It is further agreed that in the division of such waters during the irrigation season, between the 1st of April and 31st of October, inclusive, annually the United States is entitled to a prior appropriation of 500 cubic feet per second of the waters of the Milk river, or so much of such amount as constituting three-fourths of its natural flow, and that Canada is entitled to a prior appropriation of 500 cubic feet per second of the flow of St. Mary river, or so much of such amount as constitutes three-fourths of its natural flow.
The channel of the Milk river in Canada may be used at the convenience of the United States for the conveyance, while passing through Canadian territory, of waters diverted from the St. Mary river. The provisions of article II. of this treaty shall apply to any injury resulting to property in Canada from the conveyance of such waters through the Milk river.
The measurement and apportionment of the water to be used by each country shall from time to time be made jointly by the properly constituted reclamation officers of the United States and the properly constituted irrigation officers of His Majesty under the direction of the International Joint Commission.
I think the mere reading of that article will show how important will be the duties which this commission will have to perform with respect to the control of the apportionment of the waters of the Milk! and St. Mary's rivers. The intention of the high contracting parties as expressed in the treaty is that the waters of the two rivers are to be treated as if they were one river, and that in making an equal apportionment the commissioners shall have in mind where the waters of one stream may be used to the best advantage, and may apportion more than one-half of one portion of the stream, or of one of the streams, to one country, and less than' one-half to the other, and more than half of the other stream to the country which gets the least amount of the first-mentioned stream, so that there may be an equal apportionment of the waters of the two streams between the people of the twd countries. This is a work which must be carefully attended to, and which will require the services of experts; and it is all important that the work shall be dond in such a manner as to satisfy the people' of the two countries in order to prevent the irrigation which would naturally arise if there was a feeling on either side that any injustice was being done. I may say

for the information of the committee, that these two streams both take their rise in United States territory. The St. Mary's river rises in the mountains and runs to the northward, flowing later on into the Saskatchewan river. The Milk river also rises in the United States, not very far from the source of the St. Mary's river. It flows northeasterly across the Canadian boundary, flows easterly for about one hundred miles, then flows again to the south, passing through United States territory, and it empties into the Missouri river. So in the absence of a treaty, and if it were recognized that either country could assert its rights to the waters so far as they were within the territory of such country, the United States, if it chose to exercise those rights, might have diverted the waters of both of those rivers before they enter into Canadian territory, carry them eastward into the Marias river, and so on down to the Missouri, and thus deprive the people of Alberta of the right to use any portion of those waters which have their source in the United States.
I would like to see some authority for the position that they can do that under the principles of international law.	[DOT]
My own opinion is that there is no question about their right to do it, unless by so doing they interfered in some way with navigation in the adjoining country.

What difference in principle is there between the' right of navigation and the right to use for other purposes)? I cannot see the distinction. If they can divert so as to interfere with the use of it for irrigation, why can they not interfere with its use for navigation? What difference is there in principle? The principle which would forbid it in both cases is this, that the river runs partly through the territory of one sovereign power and partly through the territory of another sovereign power, that' both have rights in it, and that neither one of those countries can use that water to the detriment of the other. That has always been my idea. I would like to see some authority for the position the min-ter takes.

I think my hon. friend will find that the recognition of the international right to complain of the diversion of waters before they pass into its territory depends entirely upon the question of navigation. I am satisfied that if my hon. friend looks up the authorities he will find that that is the only case in which the sovereign right of a country is disputed. It is recognized that it pertains
to the sovereign right of a country to deal with waters in its own territory, just as it would deal with any other species of property, and that right, under international law, is subject to this one consideration^ that if diversion interferes with the waters in that country, if it interferes or materially affects navigation in the territory further down, the government of the country \shose navigation has been affected has a right to complain under the principles of international law against such diversion. I am satisfied my hon. friend will find that the right is limited wholly to cases where it is alleged that navigation has been seriously interfered with.

It is plain so far
as navigation is concerned that it cannot be interfered with. Both countries have rights, and neither, one can interfere with the rights of the other. I find, on looking at some of the authorities, that two or three hundred years ago the country through which the lower part of any such river ran, claimed and at one time exercised the right to prevent access to the sea by the inhabitants of the country through which the upper part of the stream ran. But that has all been done away with.
That deals with navigation.

I understand that. But what I cannot understand, and what I cannot find any authority for, after looking up the books for the last half hour, is that any country has such an exclusive right to deal with the waters of an international river. I admit that I cannot find any authority so far which says that one country cannot divert, but, on the other band, I cannot find any authority which says that any country can divert to the detriment of the other. Therefore, there being no authority so far as I can find either way, I would think that the same principle which applies to navigation of the stream would also, according to sound logic, apply to the diversion of the waters of a stream, and in the absence of any authority to the contrary I would consider that to be the law.

My hon. friend will rind a very valuable opinion given by the attorney general of the United States in a question which came up on the complaint of the government of Mexico against a diversion of a portion of the Rio Grande riveT. The question is well reasoned, and put distinctly on this ground, that it would be an interference with the sovereign right of a nation, with the right of sovereignty in a nation, for any other country to say: You shall not deal as you like with the waters in your own country, your legislature shall not have power to deal with

waters in your own country, and the right to complain upon the ground that navigation is interfered with, is an exception which is engrafted on to that principle of the recognition of the sovereign right of each country to deal with waters in its own territory. My hon. friend, I think, will find no case anywhere in which anv country has claimed to interfere with the sovereign right of another country except in cases where it is alleged that diversion has interfered with navigation-unless it may be in the case of the government of Mexico, which asserted that a whole town was destroyed, a beautiful and flourishing town,- because it was inundated by the waters either of the Rio Grande or a branch of the Rio Grande. The United States Congress, or one of the state legislatures, permitted the diversion of that water over their part of the territory, the result of which was to turn that beautiful section of Mexican territory almost into a desert. A complaint was made to the government of the United States, and the opinion of the attorney general was, a very well reasoned opinion, that it would be an interference with the sovereign right of the United States if it were to recognize that any other country had the right to say what it should permit with regard to waters in its own territory. It is laid down that no country could tolerate such interference or complaint upon the part of any other country.

I do not know what argument might have been made by the Attorney General of the United States. I would pay as much respect to that as the reasoning contained in it would demand, but I would not regard the argument of the Attorney General of the # United States, made with respect to a matter in controversy between his own government and the government of Mexico, as absolutely conclusive of the international law upon this subject. I repeat that I can see no distinction between rights which must be respected by reason of the use of a river for navigation and Tights which ought to be respected by reason of the use of the waters of a river for other purposes. My hon. friend has not pointed out any distinction. He says it is a matter that appertains to the sovereign rights of a state, but he must remember that we are speaking of rivers which in the natural course of the configuration of the country, run into the territory of another state which has equal sovereign rights with respect to the waters of that river when they come within its boundaries. The point for which my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works contends is a very important one. He has alluded to one case where a very considerable- portion of territory was rendered absolutely unproductive. His position then would be that a portion of Alberta in this Dominion, which Mr. PUGSLEY.
depends for its fertility upon waters that have their rise in the United States, could be absolutely destroyed and rendered unfit for navigation simply because those waters took their rise in the United States before they flowed into Canada. With all respect to my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works, I doubt very much if this position could be maintained. It certainly has no analogy whatever to the ordinary rule as between individuals within any sovereign state because they may use the waters that run through their lands, but they may not use them to the detriment of those above or below them. They may use them in the ordinary course. If you argue from that as to similar rights existing between sovereign powers through the territories of both of which a particular river runs, you find that the same principle should apply not only as to navigation, but also as to the use of the water of the river for any reasonable purpose that might be required by the in-' habitants in one country or the other. I do not feel myself bound at all by the opinion of the Attorney General of the United States making an argument for the interest of his own country in the matter that has been alluded to.

My view is that it would be an act of discourtesy which would be greater or less depending upon the extent of the waters which were diverted, but it would not be a casus belli. It would not be a ground upon which the government would feel warranted in taking hostile action against the government which authorized such a diversion to take place. It is different in the case of navigation. That is what I mean and I am sure that my hon. friend will not find any authority which holds that it is contrary to international law to make that diversion. However, perhaps, that is not so material now because we have provided by this treaty, or those who have had to do with the making of the treaty, have provided that there shall be an equal division of the water, that even though they naturally take their rise in the United States the water shqll be equally divided between the two countries. Then, as St. Mary's river is used quite largely for irrigation purposes in Alberta, it is provided that in the dry seasons the seasons when the water is most needed, there shall be a prior right to 500 cubic feet per second bn the St. Mary's river by the people of Alberta and there shall be 500 cubic feet prior right to the people of the United States oh the Milk river. We have secured the prior right in the water which is most important to the people of Alberta and we have allowed the United States to take the prior right in the river, namely, the Milk river, which, no doubt, has been thought to be of importance to the people of the United States, but which certainly is of very much

less importance to the people of Canada. However, I referred particularly to this article in order to show the important duties which these commissioners have to perform and as being one reason why we are asking what some might regard as a liberal salary for them. I think that even that one article would, if the commissioners had no other duties to perform, show that it would be important to have men of very great capacity and of good judgment and who would be prepared to give to the consideration of these questions the very greatest possible care.
From what the hon. gentleman says I should judge that he is satisfied that the arrangement is fair to Canada. I have no intention to discuss it.

Yes, I am, and I may say to my hon. friend before agreeing to the terms of the treaty the government gave a great deal of consideration to it. This article 6 particularly was the subject of very careful inquiry. We did not depend solely upon the information which we had from our officials, but we went outside and got information from those who were best capable of passing judgment upon the question. I can assure my hon. friend that we came, after the most careful consideration and after very full inquiry, to the conclusion that the treaty was eminently fair to Canada and that if there was any advantage to either country that advantage certainly was not against the people of Canada. Perhaps my hon. friend would think it better to discuss it later.

I have no intention of discussing it. The hon. gentleman has stated that they have gone outside to get information. They managed to go considerably outside and away from gentlemen who understood the situation in order to get the information.
Where is that?
Did the hon. gentleman call in any of the people who live in the immediate neighbourhood to tell him what they knew about the situation?
Yes.
Whom? Will the hon. gentleman tell me?

One gentleman was Mr. J. S. Dennis, who has been for twenty years prominently connected with work in that western country, who for many years has been prominently connected with irrigation work and has been in charge of the irrigation work of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. I think my hon. friend will not question his judgment.
I think, as the hon. gentleman is going to have a Bill before the House, probably it would be well to discuss it at a future day.
Who represented Canada in the negotiation of this treaty?

The British ambassador and Mr. George C. Gibbons, chairman of the Deep Waterways Commission. That is speaking as a general thing. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ayles-worth) and myself also attended at Washington to confer with the British ambassador upon this subject. This was in reference to certain questions which arose during the consideration of the draft treaty.
I do not think that any of you were very great experts on the Milk river or the St. Mary's river, if I may venture to say so much.
The great advantage the country had was that we did not think that we knew more than we did, and we sought to get the very best possible information from those who did know.
Whom?
We were advised by Mr. Campbell.
Who is he?

He is one of the experts of the department of the Interior. We were advised by Dr. King who has a very extensive knowledge of that section of the country; we were advised by Sir Thomas Shaughnessy, whose company owns a very large portion of the stock of the Alberta Irrigation Company, which is the only large company operating on the Canadian side of the boundary. We consulted with and were advised by Mr. Dennis, who, above all men in Canada, has had experience in irrigation work, and who has enjoyed for years in the very highest degree the confidence of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, in connection with the system of irrigation which they are carrying on in the province of Alberta. We were willing to get advice wherever we could get that advice from experts. We brought to bear the very best judgment we could, and I say without hesitation, that Article 6 is eminently fair to Canada, that it protects the rights of the people of Alberta and Saskatchewan, and if there is any advantage at all in it, it is not against the people of Canada.

In view of the positiveness of the minister as to the fairness of Article 6 to Canada, I want to say that I know more about that question than he does, not that I claim to be more intelligent than the hon. gentleman
I would be glad, if the hon. gentleman is going to make a speech, that he would first hear what I have to say.

I can express my views in a very few words to the committee. The hon. minister has positively stated that that article 6 is fair to Canada, and that he has had expert testimony which has enabled him to reach that conclusion. I entirely disagree with him. I am not going to make a speech, but I wish to say that I am just as positive on the other side, and I wish to go on record now that in my judgment, the hon. gentleman is entirely wrong in the view he holds.

I shall be glad to hear the reason for my hon. friends opinion at the proper time. Article 8 makes provision for the priority of the various uses to which the waters may be put, and Article 9 is a very important one and it provides
The high contracting parties further agree that any other questions or matters of difference arising between them involving the rights, obligations, or interests of either in relation to the other or to the inhabitants of the other, along the common frontier between the United States and the Dominion of Canada, shall be referred from time to time to the International Joint Commission for examination and report, whenever either the government of the United States or the government of the Dominion of Canada shall request that such questions or matters of difference be so referred.
Hon. gentlemen will see that it is a very far reaching provision, and one which, if the commissioners are qualified for the performance of their duties, will be likely to make for peaceable relations between the two countries in the future. It provides that outside of this question of boundary waters, there may be referred to these commissioners any other questions or matters of difference which involve the rights obligations or interests of either party along the common frontier, between the United States and the Dominion of Canada, and that reference may be made by either country without the consent of the other.
Whether it relates to waterways or not.

Whether it relates to waterways or not. If any question arises which in the absence of a treaty might lead to irritation between the two countries, either country may have the question submitted to the International Joint Commission, and that question must go to the commission whether either country desires it or not. In article 10 still wider provision is made and it reads:
Any questions or matters of difference arising between the high contracting parties in-Mr. MAGRATH.
volving the rights, obligations, or interests of the United States or of the Dominion of Canada either in relation to each other or to their respective inhabitants, mav be referred for decision to the International Joint Commission by the consent of the two parties, it being understood that on the part of the United States any such action will be by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, and on the part of His Majesty's government with the consent of the Governor General in Council. In each case so referred, the said commission is authorized to examine into and report upon the facts and circumstances of the particular questions and matters referred, together with such conclusions and recommendations as may be appropriate, subject, however, to any restrictions or exceptions which may be imposed with respect thereto by the terms of the reference.
You see there is first the provision that all these questions relating to boundary waters shall be referred to this commission; then it is provided that any questions arising in respect to the rights or obligations of either country along the frontier may be referred, at the request of either country, not with the consent of both, but by the wish of either. Then it goes still further and provides that any question whatever, whether relating to the frontier or to boundary waters, or to whatever it may relate, may be referred by the two countries to this tribunal. It is in a small way, perhaps not so small a way after all, a sort of a Hague tribunal to which may be referred by the consent of both parties all such questions of whatever nature or kind, which may arise between the United States and the Dominion of Canada. Then it is provided by this article:
A majority of the said commission shall have power to render a decision or finding upon any of the questions or matters so referred.
If the said commission is equally divided or otherwise unable to render a decision or finding as to any questions or matters so referred, it shall be the duty of the commissioners to make a joint report to both governments, or separate reports to their respective governments, showing the different conclusions arrived at with regard to the matter or questions so referred, which questions or matters shall thereupon be referred for decision by the high contracting parties to an umpire chosen in accordance with the procedure prescribed in the fourth, fifth and sixth paragraphs of Article XLV. of the Hague Convention for the pacific settlement of international disputes, dated October 18, 1907. Such umpire shall have power to render a final decision with respect to those matters and questions so referred on which the commission failed to agree.
Now, I think Mr. Chairman, that hon. gentlemen will agree with me that if this commission is what we hope it will be; if the gentlemen who are appointed on the part of the United States, and of the British government-the latter, of course, to be appointed on the recommendation of the Gov-

ernor in Council-if they are the right men, and if they proceed to discharge their duties animated by a desire not alone to defend the interests of the country which they represent, but to recognize the rights of the neighbouring country, it seems to me that this tribunal will be a most important one in making for permanent peace between these adjoining nations. We know that without some such tribunal, having this vast frontier extending between the Atlantic and the Pacific, there are likely in the future to be questions in regard to which the people of the two countries would not be likely to see eye to eye, and therefore it is of the very greatest possible importance that there should be a tribunal to which these questions may be referred from time to time for settlement. I think this is a great step forward in the direction of securing permanent peace between the two countries. The treaty further provides that the government of the United States shall appoint three members of the commission and the British government shall also appoint three members upon the recommendation of the Governor in Council. It is also provided that each section of the commission shall appoint its secretary, and that the commission may appoint such other parties, engineers, and others, -as may be necessary in order to enable them to properly discharge their duties, and also, that any expenses which are incurred by the joint order of the United States section and the Canadian section, shall be borne equally by the two countries.
I have not referred to the clause which was added to this treaty at the instance of the Senate of the United States, as I do not think it necessary to do so. My object now is not so much to justify the conclusion of this treaty as it is to endeavour to show the committee that, the treaty being concluded, the duties of the commission will be important, and that therefore the House ought to entrust the government with sufficient funds to enable them to secure men who will be fit for the discharge of the important duties which, under the treaty, will be entrusted to them. I may say, however, with regard to that clause which was added as a rider to the treaty at the instance of the Senate of the United States, that in the opinion of the Minister of Justice, who gave the matter very careful consideration, it in no way took away or disturbed the Tights of any of the people of Canada, It simply preserved certain private rights, just as the treaty leaves the private rights of the people of Canada at the Sault as they were before, and, after consideration, the Minister of Justice gave the opinion that there was nothing in that which ought to interfere with the Canadian government approving of the treaty. Now, having explained the provisions of the treaty, I 29*
think hon. gentlemen will agree with me that if we are to have the treaty carried out satisfactorily to the people of Canada, it is desirable that we should get the very best men who are available for the purpose.
What is to be the tenure of their appointment?

They will be appointed at the pleasure of His Majesty. The resolution provides that the salary shall not exceed $7,500 per annum, which, considering the duties they have to perform, will not be considered excessive.
How long will the treaty last?

It will last for five years and thereafter until terminated by either party on 12 months' notice. I trust that the results of the treaty and the manner in which it will be administered on the part of both countries will be such that it will last, if not for ever, at least for many generations.

If I understand the minister correctly, this treaty does not contemplate any compensation being made to Canada or to any province thereof on account of the diversion from the St. John river of the Allegash water, which naturally ought to flow into it. The minister stated that it was generally recognized as a principle of international law that the country in which a river originated had sovereign rights over the water in that river and could divert that water to any purpose it pleased. _
Unless it interfered with navigation.

Well, I take it that the people of New Brunswick never consented to any such principle as that. If my memory is correct, I think the people interested in the River St. John, into which the Allegash naturally ought to flow, at one time blew up the dam on the Allegash river, which was preventing the water of that river from flowing into the St. John river. It has been a source of quarrel and irritation ever since Maine people attempted to divert the water of the Allegash into the Penobscot river. The minister's statement, which I presume is correct, will be a great disappointment to the people who are interested in having as large a flow of water in that portion of the St. John river as possible, because the diversion of the water of the Allegash has very materially interfered with the navigation of that stream. Of course, the treaty has been signed, and any debate on it now goes for nothing. But it certainly does emphasize the importance of the people who are specially interested in a treaty such as this

being consulted before it is finally signed and made law. However, the treaty has been made and is not laid before parliament until after it has been signed, sealed and delivered; and this parliament, which ought to have something to say as to a treaty of this kind, has really had nothing whatever to say with regard to its various clauses. I do not think it is a good way to start making treaties on behalf of Canada. Where a treaty of so much importance is undertaken by the government of this country, although nominally made between His Majesty and the United States, this parliament at least ought to be consulted and have something to say with regard to its terms.

I would like to say to my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works that he evidently had not examined all the authorities when he made the rather sweeping statement that no authority could be found in opposition to the view which he presented very forcibly to the committee. I have in my hand the first volume of a treatise on international law by Prof. Oppenheim, a very well known and able writer and lecturer on international law. This gentleman is Lecturer in Public International Law at the London School of Economics and Political Science (University of London), and a member of the faculty of Economics and Political Science of the University of London, and formerly Professor Ordinarius of Law in the University of Basle, Switzerland. In the preface to the book he says:

I have nearly always taken pains to put other opinions, if any, before my readers. I have been carefeul to avoid pronouncing rules as established which are not yet settled. My book is intended to present international law as it is, not as it ought to be.
All through the book where there is any doubt as to any particular doctrine, he always presents the doubt. I am indebted for reference to this authority to my hon. friend from St. Anne (Mr. Doherty). On page 175 my hon. friend will find this:-
Just like independence territorial supremacy does not give a boundless liberty of action. Thus, by customary international law every state has a right to demand that its merchantmen can pass through the maritime belt of other states. Thus, further, navigation on so called international rivers in Europe must be open to merchantmen of all states. Thus, thirdly, foreign monarchs and envoys, foreign men-of-war, and foreign armed forces must be granted exterritoriality. Thus, fourthly, through the right of protection over citizens abroad which is held according to customary international law by every state, a state cannot treat foreign citizens passing or residing on its territory arbitrarily according to discretion as it might treat its own subjects; it cannot, for instance, compel them to 6erve in its army or navy. Thus, to give another and fifth example, a state is, in spite of its Mr. DANIEL.	j	l
territorial supremacy, not allowed to alter the natural conditions of its own territory to the disadvantage of the natural conditions of the territory of a neighbouring state-for instance, to stop or to divert the flow of a river which runs from its own into neighbouring territory.
Exactly the point we have been debating this afternoon and a direct authority against the position which the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) has taken.
Is that not in the case of a navigable river?

It says nothing of the kind, I will read it again. It cannot mean what my hon. friend sugv gests it means, because the very second example he gave was that navigation on international rivers in Europe must be open to the merchant men of all states. He is dealing with something else, something fuller and more comprehensive.
Thus to give another and fifth example, a state is, in spite of its territorial supremacy, not allowed to alter the natural conditions of its own territory to the disadvantage of the natural conditions of the territory of a neighbouring state-for instance, to stop or to divert the flow of a river which runs from its own into a neighbouring territory.
If the writer of this book had intended to use language absolutly descriptive of the very point we are debating now he could not have used any more apt for that purpose. It seems to me that the Minister of Public Works and the government must have been altogether too much influenced by the opinion of the Attorney' General of the United States in the Mexican case to which he refers and must have accepted as a thoroughly reliable statement of international law what was, after all, only an argument made by the Attorney General of the United States in opposition to a claim for damages from Mexico., I would be inclined to think that the government in entering into this treaty have! had a wrong impression as to the international law on this subject. The Minister of Public Works took pains to state that the rule of international law as he understood it was embodied in the terms of this treaty except that a right of action was provided. It would appear that international law is not embodied in the terms of this treaty, that a very different principle is laid down and recognized by this treaty, one for which my hon. friend says the United States has made contention in the past, notably in the case of a dispute with Mexico to which he alluded. I do not know that there is any particular reason why we should have been led in this particular case to accept as a true statement of international law that which was simply an argument, a brief for the*

United States, put forward by its Attorney General, whose duty it was to put forward that argument in the way which best might serve to maintain the interests of the United States. I think that my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works has not made good his position or the position of the government ; he has merely made it apparent to the House that the government, in entering into this treaty, have done so with not very much regard to international law, and as far as they did have any regard thereto, under a very thorough misapprehension as to the rules of civilized nations with regard to this subject.

The hon. member for St. John (Mr. Daniel) rather assumes that in some way this treaty interferes with the situation so far as the Allegash river is concerned. It does not touch at all the Allegash river, it only deals with boundary waters, with the exception of the Milk and St. Mary's, which are especially provided for.
Boundary waters and waters flowing into them.
Oh, no. The preliminary article is as follows.
The minister said a short time ago it had settled that question.

I said it had so far as navigation is concerned, that is to say navigation cannot by interfered with,_ but that is a right which is reserved. My statement is that the treaty expressly provides, by the preliminary article, that it does not deal with waters flowing into a boundary water. To make that plainer still, it expressly provides that nothing in_ tile treaty shall take away the right of either country to protest against any interference with navigation.
What does the first clause in Article II mean?

That each of the high contracting parties reserves all its right, that is the right to control the waters on its own side of the line. That is, by this treaty, each country reserves its right to deal with waters on its own side of the boundary line but it is recognized that it cannot deal with them in such a way as to interfere with navigation. I wish to make it clear that so far as the Allegash is concerned, this treaty does not come in at all, it leaves the question of diversion exactly where it was before. If that diversion interferes, as when I was a member of the provincial government I always contended it did interfere and as I contend to-day it did interfere with the navigation of the St. John river, this treaty
does not alter the right of the people of New Brunswick or of Canada or the government of Canada to protest against that diversion. This, however, is a diversion which took place some fifty years ago. When the diversion was fresh .before the government of the country, I presume representations were made to the British government on the subject. I presume the British government did not take it to be a casus belli, the ground for taking a hostile attitude towards the United States; it was allowed to remain and for forty years before this government came into power this diversion continued. This treaty leaves those rights exactly as they were before, it does not take away the right of the people or of the government to protest just as from time to time they have protested in the past.

Does it place in the hands of the Joint Waterways Commission power to hear these complaints and remedy them? If they find they are worthy or to endeavour to remedy them as far as the Allegash is concerned.

I would think it does so far as it might interfere with navigation.
In answer to the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden, Halifax) I think he does the government injustice when he says that we have proceeded upon a wrong theory so far as this treaty is concerned. Now, my hon. friend ought to remember,
I think, that what I pointed out was that the United States, in the case of the Republic of Mexico, had taken the ground that they had the sovereign right to divert for purposes of irrigation the water flowing through the United States and into Mex; can territory. But that they have the right to do this was not the mere opinion of the attorney general; it was the deliberate action of the government of the United States. Now, does my hon. friend suggest for a moment that, if the United States government had diverted the waters of the St. Mary's river or of the Milk river, the British government would have gone to war with the United States because of that diversion? He must recognize that it was the settled determination of the United States to maintain the sovereign right to do as they pleased with the waters of their own country, except so far as it might interfere with navigation in the neighbouring country.
Does the minister mean that because the United States insisted that that was the principle of international law we must admit at once that it was the principle of international law?
No, I do not say that.
Then, what do s the minister mean?

I say that, in my opinion, the United States is right in that contention.
Mr. BORDEN (Halifax;. Has the government accepted that contention?

No, the treaty is not framed on that theory. I was presenting that view as a reason why this treaty might be regarded even as more satisfactory . than one might regard it simply having reference to its terms, and if one were to take that view of international rights and obligations. What I said before, and what I say now, is that, apart altogether from the question of the right of either country to divert water, this provision under Article VI. is eminently fair to both countries because it provides, in respect of both these streams which take_ their rise in the United States and pass through Canadian territory, that the water shall be equally divided between the two countries, and that such division shall take place under the direction of this International Joint Commission which shall have power to divide them from time to time so as to give the most beneficial use possible to the people of both countries. So. altogether apart from the question of international rights, this treaty affords us, so far as the St. Mary's and Milk rivers are concerned, provisions eminently fair and calculated to do complete justice to the people of the two countries. I move the adoption of the resolution.

We shall come to the fairness of the provisions by and by -it may be that we could not get very far with that to-night. But the minister said, over and over again, that the principle laid down and recognized in Article 2 was a well known principle of international law. I challenged him on that point and asked for his authority. I got his reply in the reference to the attitude of the United States with regard to Mexico. I challenged him later on, and he said it would be impossible to produce any authority to sustain the contention which I respectfully put forward with all possible deference to the opposite view which he had stated. He has the authority now, and I do not think he can produce any authority in opposition to it. That indicates that the Minister of Public Works, who appears to have been particularly acting for the government in this matter, entered into the treaty without a due regard to the ordinary .principles of international law, and that it would have been better for the government to examine, have examined that matter thoroughly. Had they done so, they might have arrived at a different conclusion as to whether the article is or is not a fair settlement of the question so far as this country is concerned. However, we can discuss that later.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I take, with each one of my colleagues, the fullest responsibility for recommending the acceptance of the treaty which is under consideration. The question which had to be considered as a practical question, in coming to a conclusion on that point, was, whether or not we were better off with such an international arrangement as this is, than we should be without any at all. It is all very well for the learned leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax), to cite us the opinion of a very well known text writer, stating that a nation is not allowed to divert a river which crosses the boundary between its territory and that of another nation, if such diversion will injure property the territory of the down-stream nation. That is a very good principle ; it is exactly the principle of law which would be enforced as between an up-stream riparian owner, who was seeking to divert, and a down-stream riparian owner, who was to be hurt by it, if the two properties were in the same country. But how are you going to enforce such a provision of international law-if it be a settled principle of international law-when the property injured is in a different country from that in which the diversion takes place? Now, on this very point as to the effect of a diversion in the up-stream, a case came before the existing Waterways Commission. An undertaking in the state of Minnesota desired to do just what was done in the case of the Allegash lake or river. Water flowed in the state of Minnesota from a natural source, into the Rainy river, to ultimately find its way to the ocean through the water's of Hudson's bay.. This undertaking, being authorized thereto by the legislature of Minnesota, was proposing to take that water over an intervening height of land, and, by artificial means, carry it to the southward so that it would flow into the Mississippi and the Gulf of Mexico. That diversion was objected to on the part of Canadian riparian owners, and, in view of the objection, the existing Waterways Commission considered that very subject and came to the conclusion-the United States members of the commission agreeing-that-such a diversion ought not to take place. That was prior to this treaty altogether. That question and the reasons for the conclusion which the Waterways Commission came to, is to be found in one of their annual reports. And just by reason of that conclusion of the commission when it came to be a matter of discussing the terms of this proposed arrangement with the United States, Mr. Root, as Secretary of State of the United States, took the highest possible ground, that he would not agree to it. And it was just in this position that we could not get the stipulation which would have carried out the rule of law as to flowing wiater which is undoubtedly to

be applied supposing the riparian owners are in the same country. We thought that, inasmuch as the common law oi England is the basis alike of the law of all our Canadian provinces, except Quebec, and of the various boundary states of the United States, we might well appeal to that common law and might well urge that, just as in either Ontario -or any of the border states of the Union no downstream owner would be allowed to be in jured by an up-stream diversion, nor any up-stream owner allowed to be flooded out and submerged by some down-stream obstruction, so the same rule ought to apply in all flowing streams whether flowing out of the United States into Canada or out of Canada into the United States. And, speaking for myself, I will say at once, that I would have been much better pleased if that rule had been applied.
But when you are making a bargain of any kind, whether it be an international treaty or a compromise between two individuals, you have got to get the best terms you can secure, and frequently you have to compromise, and do a considerable amount of give and take. Now, we could not induce the representatives of the United States in this matter to go the length we would like to go, the length of declaring the principle of common law that water flows and ought to be allowed to flow. But we have induced them to go a considerable distance. Supposing they had been willing to affirm the principle that I have alluded to, and to declare that there should be no diversion, then what would have been the remedy? The right of the down-stream man would have been either to prevent a diversion up stream which would hurt him, or to have compensation paid him for injury if that diversion was allowed to take place. We could not induce the United States to go the length of preventing the injury, of giving our Canadian down-stream owner a right to enjoin the intended diversion up-stream. It was said that no diversion could take place except by legislative authority, no matter whether that diversion was in Canada or in the United States, and it is not right that a sovereign legislature, whether in Canada or the United States, should be restrained from doing what it thinks is in the interest of its people. Therefore there cannot be any question of preventing a diversion if a legislature decides upon it. But wherever a diversion takes place, on whichever side of the boundary, if the effect is to injure the property of a riparian down-stream owner in the other country, we will agree to put that man in exactly the same position he would have been in if there had been no boundary at all. If there had been no boundary, if that property, instead of being the first lot, if you please, on
the Canadian side of the boundary, had been the last lot on the United States side, the owner could not prevent the up-stream diversion because it was 'something permitted by his legislature. You could not expect to put the Canadian down-stream owner on a higher footing than the United States down-stream owner himself. If the diversion is permitted up-stream by authority of the legislature of one of the United States, then no down-stream man can prevent it, but he is entitled to compensation. The agreement is: We will put the Canadian down-stream man on precisely the same footing and give him precisely the same rights to compensation as United States citizens have, put him exactly in the position he would have been in if the boundary had been away to the north of him, instead of between him and.the diversion, or putting the boot on the other foot, it would have been perfectly possible in a physical situation for Canadians to have obstructed the waters of the Milk river where they flow through Canada, or to have taken out for irrigation, or other purposes, such quantities of those waters as would have been an injury to the United States riparian owners further down the Milk river after it returns across the 49th parallel into the United States. Now, if it were something not specially provided for in the 6th clause of this treaty, if we had only the 2nd clause, if they did that, they would be liable for damages exactly as if the whole stream had been in the one territory. They could not prevent it, no injunction would lie to restrain them. But in either point of view the citizen on each side of the boundary line is put exactly on the same footing, and looking at the thing from that standpoint, it seems fair. I fully concede, as I have said, that if we could have got the right to prevent diversions, even though that would have subjected us in Canada, to some restraint upon diversions we might like to make, I would have been personally better pleased, and would have thought that it was more fully carrying out the principle of the common law. But unable to get that, we have got certainly the next best thing, and a very great advance upon nothing at all, because if there had been no treaty you could not have prevented the United States doing these very same things. It is all very well to cite Oppenheim to them, but what do they care for Oppenheim when there* is no court to enforce the rules of law he lays down? You could not have any redress short of an agreement to go to the Hague. The utmost we could do would be to expostulate, to complain, to grumble, to protest, and what good would it have done us? I think, taking a practical view of the situation, that it was wiser to take what we could get than to refuse and get anything at all.

The argument of the Minister of Justice, when it is reduced to its last analysis, seems to amount to this; whatever the attitude of the United States may be with regard to matters of great international import, we are obliged to accept it, because we can do nothing but expostulate. The present is perhaps not a very serious illustration. The United States have taken very high ground in international matters before ; we have not always accepted it. They took the ground that they had a right to capture Canadian vessels on the high seas on the theory that the Behring sea was a mare clausum, but that was not accepted. There was expostulation, and the expostulation eventually was so effective that the matter was referred to an impartial tribunal. I am not pretending for a moment to say that this is a case which equals in gravity the one to which I have alluded, but they are much alike in principle. I would not be inclined exactly to accept the view which the Minister of Justice puts forward, namely that when an attitude is taken by the United States in disregard of accepted authorities on international law, we are obliged to recognize that as a sound position simply because if we do not, nothing will be left to us but to expostulate.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speechtext:
Before the resolution is carried I want to say a few words about the resolution itself. I am pleased that the discussion on the treaty for the present is disposed of, because it is not an agreeable subject with me, and in so far as I am concerned, in regard to the resolution providing $75,000 for this service, I am quite prepared to support it. These commissioners are going to be called upon to look after the inter-

ests of this country in one of its greatest assets. We want to secure men on that commission whose scientific attainments enable them to look into the faces of men prepared to do business for any other country, I am not going to suggest to the committee that to-morrow morning $7,500 per year is going to be a target for men throughout this country looking for jobs. I merely want to place myself on record now before that commission is appointed. I am quite satisfied that the individual members should get $7,500 a year, but I ask the government to keep that feature in mind and to get scientific men who can stand up and face the representatives of the United States and do business for this country. I feel, Mr. Chairman, and I feel very strongly in connection with this treaty we have been discussing that that feature was not sufficiently looked after.
Will these commissioners have the power to grant the right to dam a navigable stream such as the St. Lawrence, say at the Long Sault or the Cedar rapids, without coming to parliament?

My hon. friend surely does not feel it necessary to ask that question. There is nothing in the treaty which gives the Joint Commission the power to authorize the damming of the St. Lawrence. That authority could only be given by this parliament and all that this treaty provides for is that even if this parliament *were to give authority then, in so far as boundary waters are concerned, there must be the approval of the Joint Commission.
I am glad to hear that. It was rumoured that they would have such power.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Do not believe rumours.
I would like to know if the minister will lay the regulations or instructions that the commission will receive on the table of the House, or make parliament acquainted with them.

That would be entirely the right thing to do. I can assure my hon. friend that any regulations which may be made and which will necessarily be made by the Governor General in Council will be submitted to parliament.
And the instructions to the commissioners?
Yes.

I do not understand this exactly yet. Take, for instance, the Long Sault with regard to which we had so much trouble last year. If the United States decide to dam what is called
the South Sault rapids which are entirely on the American side of the river-in fact the whole of the Long Sault rapids are on the American side with the exception of a very small portion on the Canadian side- can they do so, if they get the approval of this commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They can do it now without the approval of anybody.

As I understand it you cannot dam any part of the St. Lawrence river without the consent of both countries-Canada and the United States, the South Sault is a navigable part of the St. Lawrence river, and this same company which wants to dam the St. Lawrence at the Long Sault now intends, I am told, to dam it at the South Sault. If they get the consent of the state of New York to that and also the consent of this commission, will it be unnecessary for them to get the consent of this parliament.

I think it is clear that they could not do it hereafter unless they can do it now, without coming to this parliament. This treaty is restrictive, not permissive. It does not give to any company any right which it does not now enjoy, and in order that the rights of the people of both countries shall be safeguarded it is provided that these questions shall be submitted to the International Joint Commission. No person and no company can get any power from this commission to do what by law they are not authorized to do. They must come either to the legislature of the state of New York or to this parliament and get authority to place any works in that boundary river. Were it not for this treaty they probably could get the authority from the legislature or parliament of either country to construct works upon their own side of the river, but no company can get any authority in that respect from this Joint Commission. As I say, it is restrictive and not permissive, and it is intended to safeguard the public interest by providing that even after legislative authority is obtained they must submit their plans to the commission and get the approval of the commission. But, this commission cannot give any authority or any approval unless authority is first obtained from the legislature having power to grant it.

There is the North Sault, where the Richelieu and Ontario steamers go down, and there is the South Sault rapids, which are run every day by smaller steamers of say 200 tons burden. I am informed by competent legal authority here that if the United States give authority to dam the St. Lawrence or any navigable stream on their side of the river, if authority is also obtained

from this commission, there would be no necessity for coming to this parliament. Now, if they could dam the South Sault rapids they would probably injure for all time to come the Cornwall canal, and they would destroy the North Sault rapids. I am perfectly satisfied if this commission has no power to grant permission to parties in the United States to dam any por->
tion of the St. Lawrence river which is now a navigable stream, but, competent legal authority on this side is of the opinion that if they wish to place a dam for power purposes entirely within the United States, they can go ahead with it if they get the consent of the proper legislative authority in the United States and of this commission.
What would these legal authorities say and do at present, before the commission is appointed?

They say that under the treaty between Great Britain and the United States, the United States cannot dam any portion of the St. Lawrence at the point I have mentioned without getting the consent of the Dominion of Canada.
Under what treaty?

The Ashburton treaty. Now, if without the consent of this parliament, they can get 200,000 horsepower by damming the Sault, we would get no revenue from the sale of that power and the United States would reap all the advantage. Under the Ashburton treaty no portion of the St. Lawrence river between the two countries can be dammed at the present time without the consent of the Canadian government and the legislative authority in the United States, whether it be the legislature of New York or the federal government. We should be very careful to guard whatever power we give to this commission in this respect. A few years ago the Canadian government gave permission to a company at Massena to run a canal at the Sault rapids from which power is obtained and from which we get no revenue.
Do you say that this government granted that permission?
This government gave them permission to take off a canal from the St. Lawrence river, the result of which was to turn the water in another direction.
Did they restore the water to the river?

What they did was to dig a canal from the South Sault rapids into the Racket river. If that dam Mr. REID.
was to break away or Tie destroyed the water would be forced through that canal and perhaps destroy the navigation of both the North Sault and the South Sault.
Was that authority given by this parliament, and, if so, when?
It was given by the department.
I think my hon. friend is misinformed.
I understood that from a party connected with this power company.
It would be very much better to find out from the order or the statute what was done.

At all events, I would like the Prime Minister, in this case, to guard against any possibility of trouble between the United States and Canada in regard to damming the St. Lawrence at this particular point without our having a full opportunity to discuss the matter in parliament.
Does the hon. gentleman know', as a fact, that the w'ork does exist there?
I know that this canal does exist.
On the American side?
On the American side.

My hon. friend must see the absurdity of this. How could this government give authority to anybody to build a canal on the American side of the boundary line? The very statement of my hon. friend show's that he must be wrong. I can understand the United States government giving the authority, but not this government.

The United States government did give the authority to dredge a canal from the St. Lawrence, but before the company proceeded with the work they asked for the consent of the Public Works Department of this government, and got it. The South Sault rapids are entirely in the United States, and 95 per cent of the North Sault rapids are in the United States, and if this Bill is going to give the company authority to dam the South Sault rapids without coming to parliament, I certainly object to that. The hon. minister told us last year that he was protecting Canadian interests when he was getting $30,000 a year as a rental for damming the whole St. Lawrence river at Cornwall.
My hon. friend is wrong. Nothing of the kind took place. My hon. friend is simply feeding on his imagination.

When we raised the question of damming the St. Lawrence the hon. minister made the statement that he was protecting the interests of Canada because we were going to get $30,000 a year of revenue from that, similar to what the United States was getting.

Not at all. Surely my hon. friend ought not to make these statements without trying to get at the facts. There was no proposition to dam the St. Lawrence, though gentlemen opposite tried to make people believe there was, and then they, were astonished to find that those who were promoting the Bill were willing to accept any amendment to make it clear beyond the shadow of a doubt. What I stated was that if parliament should hereafter grant any authority to dam the St. Lawrence and I were Minister of Public Works at the time, I would see that any company getting the power would pay as much as was to be paid to the state of New York, which I understood was to be $30,000 a year.
Does the hon. gentleman mean to say that no proposal was made to him last year to dam the St. Lawrence?
None whatever.
If I remember, the hon. gentleman said that the plans were referred to him, and that he approved of them.
Not at all. I disapproved of the plans, and then they were referred to the International Waterways Commission.
I do not see how the proposal could be rejected if it was not made.

However, the only thing I want the Prime Minister to assure the House is that if this commission is appointed, it will not have the power to authorize the damming of the rapids at Cornwall until it comes to this House and gets the power to do so. Will the Prime Minister agree to that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not understand what my hon. friend asks me. The treaty is there, this is only the first day, and the Bill will have to come for its first, second and third readings, so that there will be plenty of opportunity for discussion.

I would like to know if there has been any correspondence with regard to this treaty which has not been brought down?
c r WILFRID LAURIER. Everything has been brought down. However, I will look again, and if there is any that has not 1 een brought down, I will bring it down.

I would like to have the assurance that it will be brought down, if there is any, before this measure goes to another stage. I would like also to know if there is any understanding between this government and the United States government with respect to the legislation that shall be passed in both countries for the purpose of making the treaty effective.

So far as I am aware, the only legislation on the part of the United States has been the making of provision at the last session of Congress for the identical amount we are asking for, $75,000, for the salaries of the commissioners, the salary of the secretary, and other expenses. A Bill was introduced in the Senate _ by Mr. Cullom, Chairman of the Committee on Foreign Relations, along the same lines as we are proposing to-night, that is fixing the salaries of the commissioners at an amount not exceeding the salaries to be paid by the government of Great Britain and not exceeding $7,500 per annum, fixing the salary of the secretary at an amount not exceeding $3,000 a year and making the same provision for clerical and engineering assistance and the payment of one-half the expenses, just as we are doing. The Bill passed the American Senate but it did not proceed further at the last session. Whether that was because we had informed the United States authorities, through the British ambassador, that we would not be able to fake the matter up at the last session of parliament, but would have to deal with during the present session, I do not know, but they have made the same provision as we are making by this Bill so far as expenses are concerned.

I would like the minister to pronounce definitely on the statement made by the hon. member for Grenville (Mr. Reid), before we advance this matter another stage. That hon. gentleman's position is that supposing the Americans grant certain rights on one side of the St. Lawrence, taking the St. Lawrence as an instance, then can this Joint Commission sanction that work or will it be necessary as heretofore, for these parties to come and get the concurrence of the parliament of Canada? I understood the Minister of Public Works to say that he thought not. It is too important a question to leave in that way. I would ask the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Justice to tell ns definitely when we meet again, that no such right will be vested in this Joint Commission, because I feel that such a right could not be safely vested in any joint commission. If the minister can assure us of that, well and good, but it would be an unfortunate condition of things if, by anything that we are

doing now, we should change the control over these international waterways.

There is no difficulty in giving that assurance to this extent that this commission cannot take the place of parliament. There is nothing in this treaty to give them power to take the place of parliament. This treaty provides a safeguard which did not formerly exist. In all cases where it was necessary to come to parliament it will still he necessary to come to parliament. The appointing of this commission is more as a safeguard, it provides an additional safeguard. It is that if any company gets the requisite legislative authority in any matter relating to boundary waters or affecting boundary waters in any way, they must, in addition to that, get the permission of this International Joint Commission, but there is nothing that will enable this commission to take the place of parliament, and where-ever heretofore, it was necessary to get the authority of parliament, it will still be necessary to get that authority. That is, as far as it seems to me it would he possible for me to go. I cannot give an opinion as to what would be the authority of the legislature of New York to give rights on their side of the river. We know that this parliament has given authority to construct works on the Canadian side of the St. Lawrence, without going to the Unitea States. The Sheiks' Island dam is wholly on the Canadian side, and the sole authority to construct this dam was given years ago, by this parliament. It seems to me that all my hon. friend should ask, is that we should be clearly able to give an assurance that this commission does not take the place of parliament, it can confer no power which has to be conferred by parliament and in every case where, but for this treaty and the appointing of the commission, it would be necessary to come to parliament, it will still be necessary to do so. The commission can give no rights, the whole duty and scope of its authority will be of a restrictive and safeguarding character, rather than in the way of granting any permission or rights.
I shall not bandy words with the minister at this hour of the night on this point, but I may point out to the minister that we want something more than the mere statement of the minister.
The hon. gentleman is a good lawyer, he would know himself.

I have not given the matter special study. Perhaps when it comes up again I shall have given it more study. I want to know from the minister how he shows from the wording of the treaty that it is so. The minister says we have the right to construct certain Mr. LENNOX.
works on our side of the boundary, Sheik's island was mentioned. Will this commission affect that right in any way? Take a work which we would have a right to construct on our side of the boundary and the United States would have, a_ right to construct on their side of the river. Would this commission have any control over that?
Yes?
They would have the right to veto that legislation, would they not?

I would think if authority was given by this parliament to construct any works in the St. Lawrence river, the United States might say: This is going to interfere with the right of navigation or with our rights upon our side of the river and we would ask that that be referred to the International Commission.
