In the same way if the United States Congress, of the legislature of New York gave authority to construct any works on the American side of the St. Lawrence, the Canadian government would have a right to say: We would like to have this referred to the International Commission, we think it may affect-our interests, and it would go to the International Joint Commission who would have a right to determine whether the work should be permitted or not, or as to any remedial works which might be necessary in order to preserve navigation.
Each country has the right to the full navigation of its international boundary rivers, I suppose.
Yes.

Then any work constructed by the people of Canada upon their side of the river necessarily control to that extent the navigation of the river; if it encroaches on the waters at all it narrows the passage which vessels would have the right to use. Is that not the case? To that extent it interferes with navigation, and the United States would have the right to complain of it. Then that commission could say as I understand it, I am not saying whether it is right or wrong, but as I understand the minister, that commission would have the right to step in and say: Canada has no right to pass that legislation in reference to improvements upon their side of the river, or the development of power because it will interfere with the navigation rights which are vested in common in the people of the United States, and in the people of Canada. That is correct, is it not?
I should say so. That was the very object of the commission- to settle these difficulties that might arise between the two countries.

Is it quite fair to say that the only power that has anything to say about what is done on the American side of the river is, first the American legislative authority and then this commission? I am not in a position to state whether this parliament has anything to say about constructions on the American side or not ; but it seems quite clear that, in the future, under this treaty, this parliament will have no power in the matter.

I understand my hon. friend (Mr. Doherty) to say that at the present time the American legislative authority provide for work on the American side of the river and we at present would have nothing to say about it.
I say that, whether we now have any such power or not, under this treaty we shall clearly not have it any longer.

As I understand it, so far as any governmental action on this side is concerned giving authority to erect works in navigable waters, on the American side, of course, this commission would take that place. But, in every case where, to-day, it is necessary to get the authority of the Canadian parliament for any works, it will still be necessary to come to parliament. My hon. friend must see that, in this commission, there is an additional safeguard, as it is necessary to secure the approval of the commission for such works.

That is precisely what I do not see. If to-day there is power in this parliament to say anything about what construction shall he made on the American side-I am not saying there is such power-it will disappear under this treaty. So, what the minister said a few minutes ago, that it was immaterial, that whatever power parliament had now it would still have, seems to .me to be correct only if there is no power in this parliament to say anything about constructions on the American side. If we have no such power, we get the additional safeguard of the commission. But if, as suggested, by the hon. member for Grenville (Mr. Reid), a construction that would interfere with the navigability of the river, even if on the American side, could only be made with our consent, that power disappears under this provision of the treaty.
My hon. friend will hardly say that the Canadian parliament had no right, years ago, to give authority to build that dam between Sheik's island and the main land in the St. Xawrence.
That is entirely different.
It is different because it is on the Canadian side?
Let me explain the position-
Is not the channel between Sheik's island and the mainland part of the St. Lawrence river?
It is part of the canal system. The Cornwall canal runs from Dickinson's Landing to Cornwall, and Sheik's island is away below the head of it. It is not in a navigable stream.
But is it not part of the St. Lawrence?
No.
Certainly.
By what authority did the Canadian parliament authorize the building of the Cornwall canal and divert a portion of the water of the St. Lawrence river?
Botli Sheik's island and the main shore are on the Canadian side.
But is not the south shore of the river American territory?
The minister does not understand the location.
But the hon. gentleman can tell me whether it is or is not American territory.
The south shore is, yes.

At this point on the Canadian side, these works were constructed by authority of the parliament of Canada, without asking permission from the authorities of the United States. I do not know that anybody ever disputed our right. Well, if the Canadian parliament could do that in respect of our side of the boundary, the United States could equally do it in respect of their side. The object of this treaty as I have said, is to safeguard the interests of the people on both sides and provide that works in these navigable waters shall not be constructed except after obtaining the approval of the International Commission.
The portion of the St. Lawrence of which the minister speaks was not a navigable part of the St. Lawrence and is not navigable except through the canal system.
That does not affect the point.

We can consider that later. But, as a matter of fact, it is not a navigable stream. The Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) knows

that both the North and South Sault rapids have always been navigable and large steamers go down both. A steamer of probably 100 or 150 tons runs down there once or twice a week. Another thing is that, for the last fifty years, the South Sault rapids is the only one down which timber rafts go, and so the South Sault rapids are as important as the North Sault. Now, as I understand the Minister of Public Works, if the Ashburton treaty gives the United States power to dam this portion of the St. Lawrence, or any portion of that river, without coming to this parliament, it is all right. But, if we have any authority over that matter, if at a point where the river flows between the two countries we have the right to say whether a dam shall or shall not be made, it is certainly objectionable to hand that power over to a commission so that works can be made by their authority without coming to this parliament. Right at this particular point where they proposed last year to dam the St. Lawrence is the very point where the United States territory stops. From that down to Montreal the St. Lawrence is entirely in Canadian territory. I feel that the power to dam the St. Lawrence should remain entirely in the hands oi this House. The time may come when it may be necessary for us to consider the damming of the St. Lawrence, and I wish to protect the rights we now have to dam the St. Lawrence at any point, whether at Cornwall or elsewhere. I understand this treaty will place in the hands of the commission the right to issue charters to dam the St. Lawrence at the South Sault, for instance, and this government would have to sanction it. If this government ever gives the right to dam the South Sault rapids it will not only destroy the channel of the North Sault, but I believe it will destroy the Cornwall canal.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This treaty does not confer the slightest legislative authority upon the board of commissioners. There is no fear whatever that they will give any such permission as my hon. friend speaks of. In addition to getting such legislative authority as any such proposed enterprise would now require, they will, under this treaty, require to get the approval of the commission as well.
Resolution reported and agreed to.
Mr. PUGSLEY moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 36), relating to the establishment and expenses of the International Joint Commission under the Waterways Treaty of January 11, 1909.

Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.
On motion of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, House adjourned at 11.50 p.m.
Wednesday, December 7, 1910.
